title: Southern Fresh in Safety Harbor: The Best Fried Chicken in Tampa Bay
excerpt: Southern Fresh in downtown Safety Harbor serves the best pan-fried chicken platter in Tampa Bay. Here is why I go out of my way to eat here every time I am working Safety Harbor real estate.
content:
I sell real estate all over Tampa Bay, but I go out of my way to list and show homes in Safety Harbor. Not just because it is one of the most charming small towns on the Gulf Coast, although it absolutely is, but because every time I am there, I get to eat at Southern Fresh. And once you have had their fried chicken, you will understand why I structure entire showing days around a 4 PM reservation.

What Makes Southern Fresh Special?

Southern Fresh sits at 122 3rd Avenue North in downtown Safety Harbor, just one block off Main Street. It is a small, unassuming spot, the kind of place you might walk past if you did not know any better. Inside, it feels like eating at your grandmother's house if your grandmother happened to be a professionally trained Southern cook. The staff knows the regulars by name, the sweet tea comes in mason jars, and the food is made from scratch every single day.

Their pan-fried chicken is the star. This is not fast-food breaded chicken. It is seasoned, dredged, and pan-fried to order, crispy skin, juicy inside, seasoned perfectly. Pair it with their collard greens (slow-cooked, tender, with just the right amount of vinegar bite) and mac and cheese (creamy, homemade, the real deal), and you have a $20 meal that puts most $50 dinners to shame.

Why I Love Working Safety Harbor Real Estate

Safety Harbor is one of my favorite communities to service as a REALTOR. It is a tight-knit, walkable town with a downtown strip full of local restaurants, boutique shops, and the famous Safety Harbor Resort and Spa sitting right on Tampa Bay. The real estate market in Safety Harbor draws buyers who want character, historic bungalows, tree-lined streets, and a community that actually feels like a community.

When I have showings in Safety Harbor, I make it a point to block out time for Southern Fresh. My clients know this about me. Some of them have become regulars themselves after I brought them here during a house hunt. There is something about sharing a great meal in the town you are about to call home that makes the whole experience feel right.

What to Order at Southern Fresh

Here is what I recommend if it is your first time:

  • Pan Fried Chicken Platter the signature dish. Get two sides. You will not regret the collard greens and mac and cheese combination.
  • Smoked Wings dry-rubbed and smoked, not fried. A completely different experience and just as good.
  • Blackened Redfish when they have it, get it. Fresh Gulf catch, perfectly seasoned.
  • Banana Pudding homemade. If you skip dessert, you are making a mistake.
  • Sweet Tea proper Southern sweet tea. None of that barely-sweetened stuff.

They also do family-style fried chicken for four if you are bringing the crew. Great for a post-closing celebration.

The Details

  • Location: 122 3rd Ave N, Safety Harbor, FL 34695
  • Hours: Tuesday through Sunday, open at 3 PM (closed Mondays)
  • Price range: $15 to $30 per person
  • Reservations: Recommended, especially weekends
  • Outdoor seating: Yes, fire pit area out back
  • Website: southernfreshco.com
  • Phone: (727) 216-6341

Safety Harbor Is Worth the Drive

Whether you are looking at homes for sale in Safety Harbor, exploring the neighborhoods, or just curious about what makes this Pinellas County town so special, come see it for yourself. Walk Main Street, check out the spa, browse the shops, and then sit down at Southern Fresh for the best fried chicken you have ever had.

And if you want to talk real estate while we eat, even better. That is literally my favorite way to work. Call me at (813) 733-7907 and I will meet you there.

Barrett Henry is a Broker Associate with REMAX Collective with 23+ years of real estate experience. He serves buyers and sellers across all 8 Tampa Bay counties from offices in Tampa, Brandon, and Largo.

title: How to Check Permits Before Buying a Tampa Home
excerpt: Which portal to search for City of Tampa vs Hillsborough County permits, how to spot unpermitted additions, and what to do in your inspection period.
content:
Quick Answer

How do I check building permits on a Hillsborough County home?

Use HillsGovHub at hcfl.gov for permits issued after January 2021. For older records (2005-2021), use the county's Building Permits Reports page. Search by property address or folio/parcel number. Look for open permits, missing final inspections, and unpermitted work.

Why Permit History Matters When Buying a Home

Permit history tells you what work was done to a house, and more importantly, whether it was done legally. In Hillsborough County, every major project needs a building permit: roof replacements, HVAC installations, water heaters, electrical panels, additions, even window replacements. If a seller tells you they put on a new roof in 2022, there should be a permit to back it up.

Unpermitted work creates real problems. Your homeowners insurance may not cover damage related to unpermitted improvements. When you go to sell, the next buyer's inspector will flag the same issues. And if the county discovers unpermitted work, they can require you to bring everything up to code, at your expense, even though you weren't the one who did the work.

First, make sure you are searching the right system

This is the mistake I see most often, and it produces a false clean result.

If the property is inside City of Tampa limits, the county portals will not have your building permits. The City issues its own. If the property is in unincorporated Hillsborough County, the county portals are correct. Temple Terrace and Plant City run their own permitting too.

So step one is not searching. Step one is determining the jurisdiction. Look up the parcel on the Hillsborough County Property Appraiser site and check the municipality field, or simply check whether the mailing city matches an incorporated city. A Seminole Heights address is a City of Tampa address even though plenty of people describe it as "Tampa" the same way they describe Brandon as "Tampa."

How to search City of Tampa permits

The City of Tampa uses the Accela Citizen Access portal at aca.tampagov.net. The City's Construction Services Division, part of Development and Growth Management, issues building permits and performs inspections inside city limits.

  1. Go to the portal and choose the Building module. You do not need an account for a basic search. An account is only required to submit an application or schedule an inspection.
  2. Search by address, permit number, or contractor name.
  3. Enter only the street number and street name. This is the part that trips people up. Leave off the direction, the suffix and the unit. Searching "2905 N Central Ave" often returns nothing while "2905 Central" returns the records.
  4. Open each record and look at the status, the final inspection, and the scope of work described.
  5. Repeat with address variations. Older properties frequently have records filed under slightly different spellings.

If the portal returns nothing at all for an older house, that is a finding, not a conclusion. Call the Construction Services Center and ask whether there are microfilm or archived records that are not in the online system. Pre-digital permits often are not.

Compare the property appraiser's square footage to the listing

This is the single fastest way to find unpermitted work, and it takes about two minutes.

The Hillsborough County Property Appraiser publishes heated area and building characteristics for every parcel. Pull that up next to the listing.

  • Listing says 1,850 sq ft, appraiser says 1,450 sq ft. That 400 square foot gap is something. An enclosed garage, a Florida room converted to living space, a rear addition, or a converted porch. Now go find the permit for it.
  • Bedroom or bathroom count differs. A fourth bedroom that the appraiser does not show usually means a converted garage or a divided room.
  • The appraiser shows a higher number than the listing. Less common, usually a data error, still worth asking about.

Why the gap matters: the appraiser's heated area generally reflects permitted, finished living space. An agent's square footage sometimes reflects a tape measure. When they disagree, a permit is usually the explanation, and the absence of one is the problem.

One important caveat. The appraiser's records are not a permit database and they do contain errors. A discrepancy is a reason to search permits, not proof of a violation.

Why unpermitted work actually hurts you

People treat this as a paperwork technicality. It is not. It hits you in four places:

  • Insurance. A carrier can deny a claim on unpermitted construction, and some will decline the policy outright. If an unpermitted addition burns or floods, you may be uninsured for that portion of the house.
  • Appraisal. Appraisers are generally instructed not to give value to unpermitted square footage. You can pay for 1,850 feet and be appraised at 1,450, which creates an appraisal gap you have to cover in cash.
  • Financing. If the appraisal comes in short because of unpermitted area, your loan amount drops with it.
  • Resale and enforcement. You inherit the problem. Code enforcement can require permitting after the fact or removal, and retroactive permitting means opening walls for inspection. On your way out, your buyer runs the same search you are running now.

Florida requires a permit for most construction, alteration, repair and addition work under Fla. Stat. 553.79 and section 105.1 of the Florida Building Code, with narrow exemptions.

Seminole Heights and Tampa Heights bungalows

These neighborhoods deserve their own note because the housing stock almost guarantees this issue.

Much of Seminole Heights and Tampa Heights was built in the 1910s through 1940s. A century of owners means a century of modifications, most of them done before anyone kept searchable records, and many done without permits in eras when enforcement was looser.

What I specifically check on a bungalow in these areas:

  • Rear additions and back-of-house kitchens. The most common unpermitted change. Original bungalows had small kitchens; almost all of them have been pushed out.
  • Enclosed front or side porches. A screened porch converted to conditioned space changes the heated area and frequently was never permitted.
  • Garage and carport conversions, often into a bedroom, an office, or an unpermitted second unit.
  • Detached structures used as living space. A garage apartment or converted shed is a zoning question as well as a permit question.
  • Electrical and plumbing from the original build. Knob and tube is rare here but galvanized supply lines are not. See what fails a Florida 4-point inspection, because an insurance decline in these neighborhoods is usually about systems, not permits.
  • Historic district overlay. Parts of these areas sit in local historic districts with design review requirements. That changes what you can alter and how, separate from permitting.

None of this makes a bungalow a bad buy. I like these houses. It means you budget a real inspection period and you do the permit search before you spend money, not after.

What to do during your inspection period

  1. Day one: confirm the jurisdiction, then search the correct portal. Pull the appraiser record at the same time.
  2. Day one: compare appraiser heated area, bedroom and bath count against the listing. Note every discrepancy.
  3. Day two or three: walk the house with the inspector and point at the discrepancies specifically. Ask "was this permitted" about each one.
  4. If you find an open or expired permit: ask the seller to close it out before closing. An open permit can hold up your own future permits and is the seller's mess to resolve.
  5. If you find unpermitted work: get a written quote for retroactive permitting from a licensed contractor before your inspection period ends, so you are negotiating with a number rather than a worry.
  6. If records are missing entirely: call the permitting office and ask about archives before you treat silence as a clean history.

The sequence matters. Everything above happens in the first few days, because the only leverage you have is an inspection period that has not expired.

How to Search HillsGovHub (Records After January 2021)

HillsGovHub is the county's current portal for building permits and inspections. No login required, it's a public search.

  • Go to hcfl.gov and find the HillsGovHub portal
  • Select Building Records
  • Search by Site Address, enter the street number and name
  • You can also search by Parcel Number (the folio number from the property appraiser)

For each permit, you'll see the permit number, type (building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing), description, application and issue dates, status, contractor name and license number, and the job value. Click into any permit to see the full inspection history, every inspection with its result and date.

How to Search Older Records (2005 to January 2021)

Records from before January 19, 2021 are NOT on HillsGovHub. They're on a separate county page called Building Permits Reports. Search the same way, by address or folio, but know that the interface is different and older.

This matters because a house built in 2013, for example, would have its original construction permits, any early repairs, and warranty-period fixes in the older system. The newer system only picks up from 2021 forward. You need to check both systems to get the full picture.

What to Look For, Red Flags

Open or Expired Permits

An open permit means work was started but never received a final inspection. An expired permit means the permit was issued but the work was never completed or inspected within the allowed timeframe. Both are problems. The county may require the current owner (that's you, if you buy it) to close out those permits, which could mean paying for inspections, corrections, or even redoing work.

HVAC and Roof Permits

These are the big ones. A new air conditioning system or a full roof replacement without a permit means the work wasn't inspected. For AC, that raises questions about whether the system was properly sized, connected, and meets code. For roofs, an unpermitted reroof can void your insurance entirely in Florida.

Missing Final Inspections

A permit that shows "issued" but no final inspection passed is essentially the same as unpermitted work from an insurance and code perspective. The work was started but never verified.

Water Heater and Electrical Work

Water heater replacements require permits. Gas-to-electric conversions require both plumbing and electrical permits. Electrical panel upgrades need permits. If you see these improvements in the home but no matching permits, that's a conversation you need to have with the seller before closing.

What I Do for My Clients

I pull permit history on every property my buyers are seriously considering. It takes 15 minutes and can save you thousands. I check both the HillsGovHub system and the older records, cross-reference what's in the inspection report, and flag anything that doesn't match. If there's an open permit from 2018 or a roof with no permit, I want to know before you're under contract, not after.

If you're looking at homes in Riverview, Brandon, Valrico, or anywhere in Hillsborough County, call me at (813) 733-7907 and I'll walk you through the permit history on any property you're considering.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to check permits before buying a home in Florida?

It's not legally required, but it's one of the smartest things you can do. Unpermitted work can affect your insurance coverage, your ability to resell, and your liability if something goes wrong. It takes minutes to check and can save you from a costly surprise.

What happens if I buy a home with unpermitted work?

You become responsible for it. The county can require you to obtain permits retroactively, which may mean opening walls for inspection, hiring licensed contractors, and bringing everything up to current code. The seller who did the work is long gone, the obligation stays with the property.

Do City of Tampa and Hillsborough County use the same permit portal?

No, and this causes false clean results. The City of Tampa issues permits inside city limits through its Accela Citizen Access portal at aca.tampagov.net. Unincorporated Hillsborough County uses the county's own system. Temple Terrace and Plant City permit separately as well. Confirm the jurisdiction before you search.

How do I spot an unpermitted addition?

Compare the Hillsborough County Property Appraiser's heated area, bedroom and bathroom counts against the listing. A gap of a few hundred square feet usually means an enclosed porch, a converted garage, or a rear addition. Then search the permit portal for that work. Appraiser records contain errors, so treat a discrepancy as a reason to search rather than as proof.

Can my home inspector check permit history?

Most inspectors focus on the physical condition of the home, not permit records. Some will cross-reference, but don't count on it. This is something your agent should be doing independently. I check permits on every property my buyers consider, it's part of the due diligence process.

Sources

  • City of Tampa Accela Citizen Access portal (permit search by address, permit number or contractor)
  • City of Tampa Construction Services
  • Hillsborough County Building and Construction Services
  • Hillsborough County Property Appraiser (heated area and building characteristics)
  • Fla. Stat. 553.79 and Florida Building Code s.105.1 (permit requirement); Fla. Stat. 553.79(15) and FBC s.105.4 (permit expiration)

title: How to Find CDD Fees Before Buying a Florida Home
excerpt: CDD fees can add $1,000 to $4,000+ per year to your costs. Here's how to check before you buy, step by step using hillstax.org and the actual tax bill.
content:
Quick Answer

How do I find CDD fees on a Florida property?

Go to hillstax.org (Hillsborough County Tax Collector), search by folio number, and open the most recent tax bill. CDD fees appear as non-ad-valorem assessments -- separate line items below the regular property taxes. They're labeled with the district name (e.g., "South Fork CDD"). Typical CDD fees range from $1,000 to $4,000+ per year.

What Is a CDD and Why Does It Matter?

A Community Development District (CDD) is a special taxing district created by the developer of a new community to fund the infrastructure -- roads, water lines, sewer, drainage, parks, amenities, and common areas. Instead of the developer paying for all of that upfront and building it into the home price, they create a CDD that issues bonds. Homeowners then pay off those bonds through annual assessments on their tax bill.

The practical impact: a CDD adds $1,000 to $4,000+ per year to your property costs, on top of your regular property taxes, HOA fees, and insurance. That's $80 to $330+ per month that many buyers don't account for until they see their first tax bill. Your lender should factor CDD into your debt-to-income ratio, but not all buyers realize how much it adds to the monthly payment. Use the mortgage calculator to estimate your full monthly cost.

How to Check: Step by Step

Step 1: Get the Folio Number

Every property in Hillsborough County has a folio number (also called a parcel number). You can find it on the listing in the MLS, on the Hillsborough County Property Appraiser website, or just ask your agent. It looks something like: U-15-31-20-B5O-B00005-00008.0

Step 2: Go to hillstax.org

This is the Hillsborough County Tax Collector's website. Click on "Property Tax Search" and enter the folio number. This pulls up the property's tax account.

Step 3: Open the Actual Tax Bill

Click on the most recent tax bill to see every line item. The bill has two sections:

  • Ad valorem taxes -- these are your regular property taxes based on assessed value. They include county general revenue, school board, hospital authority, and other taxing authorities. Each shows a millage rate and dollar amount.
  • Non-ad-valorem assessments -- these are fixed-dollar charges that don't change with your home's value. This is where CDD fees appear, along with solid waste, stormwater, and any other special assessments.

Step 4: Look for the CDD Line

If the property is in a CDD, you'll see a line item with the district name -- like "South Fork CDD" or "FishHawk CDD" or "Waterset CDD." The dollar amount is the annual CDD assessment. Some communities have multiple CDD lines.

Send Me the Address Call (813) 733-7907

Which Communities Typically Have CDD Fees?

As a general rule, newer master-planned communities in Riverview, Wesley Chapel, Lithia, and Wimauma are more likely to have CDDs. Communities built before the mid-2000s are less likely. Here are some examples:

  • Communities WITH CDDs: FishHawk Ranch, Waterset, Epperson, Mirabay, South Fork, many newer Riverview subdivisions
  • Communities typically WITHOUT CDDs: Bloomingdale, River Hills, Buckhorn Springs, most Brandon neighborhoods, most older Valrico subdivisions

But don't assume -- always check the actual tax bill. Some communities surprise you.

CDD Fees vs. HOA Fees -- They're Not the Same

HOA fees and CDD fees are completely separate charges. HOA fees go to your homeowners association for community maintenance -- landscaping, pool, clubhouse, etc. CDD fees go to the development district to pay off infrastructure bonds. You can have both, one, or neither. Many newer communities in Tampa Bay have BOTH an HOA and a CDD, which stacks up fast.

Do CDD Fees Ever Go Away?

Yes -- eventually. CDD bonds typically have a 20 to 30 year term. Once the bonds are paid off, the CDD assessment drops significantly or goes away entirely. However, a smaller ongoing CDD assessment for maintenance of district-owned infrastructure may continue. The payoff timeline depends on when the community was developed.

How to Look Up CDD Fees by County

The process for finding CDD fees is similar across Florida, but each county has its own tax collector website. Here is how to check CDD fees in every Tampa Bay area county.

Hillsborough County

Go to hillstax.org and search by folio number. Open the most recent tax bill and look under "Non-Ad Valorem Assessments" for CDD line items. Common CDDs in Hillsborough include FishHawk, Waterset, South Fork, Triple Creek, and dozens of Riverview and Wesley Chapel communities.

Pasco County

Go to pascotaxes.com and search by parcel ID or address. Open the tax bill and look for CDD assessments under non-ad valorem line items. Pasco County has seen explosive growth in master-planned communities with CDDs, including Epperson, Bexley, Connerton, Starkey Ranch, and Mirada. Many Land O' Lakes, Wesley Chapel, and Trinity neighborhoods carry CDD assessments ranging from $1,200 to $3,500+ per year.

Pinellas County

Go to taxcollect.com (Pinellas County Tax Collector) and search by parcel number or address. CDDs are less common in Pinellas County because most communities were built before CDDs became widespread in Florida. However, some newer developments in Largo and unincorporated Pinellas may carry CDD assessments. Always check the tax bill to be sure.

Polk County

Go to polktaxes.com and search by parcel ID. Polk County has a growing number of CDD communities, especially in Davenport, Haines City, Lakeland, and Winter Haven. Developments like Champions Gate, Reunion, and Providence carry CDD fees. Typical CDD assessments in Polk range from $1,000 to $3,000+ per year.

Manatee County

Go to taxcollector.com (Manatee County Tax Collector) and search by parcel number. Master-planned communities in Parrish, Palmetto, Lakewood Ranch, and Bradenton frequently have CDDs. North River Ranch, Heritage Harbour, and multiple Lakewood Ranch villages carry CDD assessments. Fees typically range from $1,500 to $4,000+ per year.

Sarasota County

Go to sarasotataxcollector.com and search by parcel ID or address. CDDs are common in newer Sarasota County developments including Wellen Park, Venice area communities, and North Port subdivisions. Lakewood Ranch communities that extend into Sarasota County also carry CDD assessments. Typical fees range from $1,200 to $3,500+ per year.

Hernando County

Go to hernandotaxcollector.com and search by parcel number. Hernando County has fewer CDDs than its southern neighbors, but newer communities in Spring Hill and Brooksville may carry CDD assessments. As development pushes north from Tampa, expect more CDD communities in Hernando. Check the tax bill for non-ad valorem assessments.

Citrus County

Go to citruspa.org (Citrus County Property Appraiser) to find your parcel, then check the tax collector at citrusctc.com for the actual bill. CDDs are uncommon in Citrus County, but some newer developments near Crystal River, Inverness, and Homosassa may have them. Most Citrus County communities rely on HOAs rather than CDDs for community infrastructure funding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are CDD fees tax deductible?

Generally, no. CDD assessments are considered special assessments, not property taxes, and are typically not deductible on your federal income tax return. Consult a tax professional for your specific situation, but don't count on deducting CDD fees the way you deduct ad valorem property taxes.

Can CDD fees increase?

The bond portion is usually fixed, but the operations and maintenance portion can increase. So yes, your total CDD assessment can go up over time, though typically not as dramatically as HOA fee increases. Check the district's annual budget for trends.

Should CDD fees be a dealbreaker?

Not necessarily -- but you need to budget for them. A home in a CDD community with a $2,500 annual assessment costs roughly $210 more per month than an identical home without one. If you're comparing a $400K home in FishHawk (with CDD) to a $400K home in Valrico (without), the true monthly cost difference is significant. I always run the full cost comparison for my buyers so there are no surprises.

How do I find CDD fees in Pasco County?

Go to pascotaxes.com, search by parcel ID or address, and open the tax bill. CDD fees appear as non-ad valorem assessments. Common Pasco CDD communities include Epperson, Bexley, Connerton, Starkey Ranch, and Mirada. Typical Pasco CDD fees range from $1,200 to $3,500+ per year.

How do I find CDD fees in Polk County?

Go to polktaxes.com and search by parcel ID. Polk County CDD communities include Champions Gate, Reunion, and Providence in the Davenport and Haines City areas. Typical assessments range from $1,000 to $3,000+ per year.

Do all Florida counties have CDD communities?

CDDs are most common in fast-growing counties like Hillsborough, Pasco, Polk, Manatee, and Sarasota where newer master-planned communities are being built. Older, more developed counties like Pinellas have fewer CDDs. Each county's tax collector website lets you check any property for CDD assessments.

title: How to Check for Solar Panel Liens Before Buying a Florida Home
excerpt: Solar panels can be owned or leased, and a leased system comes with a lien. Here's how to check UCC filings and what to ask the seller before closing.
content:
Quick Answer

How do I know if solar panels on a house are leased or owned?

Search floridaucc.com (Florida Secured Transaction Registry) for UCC-1 filings under the homeowner's name. If there's a filing mentioning solar, photovoltaic, or energy equipment, the panels are likely leased or financed, and there's a lien on them. Owned panels free and clear won't have a UCC filing.

Why Solar Panel Liens Matter

Solar panels are increasingly common on Florida homes, and they can be a great feature, lower electric bills, environmental benefits, and potential home value increase. But there's a critical distinction every buyer needs to understand: owned panels vs. leased panels.

Owned panels are yours. They convey with the property at sale, no strings attached. Leased panels belong to the solar company. When you buy the home, you're inheriting the lease, typically 20 to 25 years of monthly payments to the solar company, plus restrictions on what you can do with your roof.

A leased system usually has a UCC-1 financing statement filed with the state, which is essentially a lien on the equipment. This can complicate your closing, affect your insurance, and limit your options if the roof needs work.

How to Search for Solar Liens

Step 1: Search floridaucc.com

Go to the Florida Secured Transaction Registry at floridaucc.com. Run a free debtor search using the current homeowner's name (first and last). Look for any UCC-1 filings that mention solar, photovoltaic, energy, or the property address.

A UCC-1 filing means a creditor (the solar company) has a secured interest in equipment at the property. Common solar companies you might see: Tesla/SolarCity, Sunrun, Vivint Solar, Sunnova, or local installers.

Step 2: Check the County Official Records

You can also search the Hillsborough County Clerk's official records at hillsclerk.com. Search by the homeowner's name and look for any recorded documents related to solar leases, power purchase agreements (PPAs), or UCC fixtures filings.

Have Questions About a Property You're Considering?

I'll pull the permits, check the tax bill, and flag anything you need to know before you make an offer.

Send Me the Address Call (813) 733-7907

Questions to Ask the Seller About Solar

  • Are the panels owned or leased? This is question number one. Get documentation.
  • If leased, what are the transfer requirements? Most solar leases require the new buyer to qualify and assume the lease. If you can't or won't, the seller may need to buy out the lease before closing.
  • What's the remaining lease term and monthly payment? A 20-year lease with 15 years remaining at $150/month is a $27,000 obligation you're taking on.
  • Is there a buyout option? Some leases allow the homeowner to purchase the system. Get the buyout price in writing.
  • What happens if the roof needs replacement? Removing and reinstalling leased panels for a reroof can cost $5,000-$10,000, and the solar company may need to coordinate the work. Who pays?
  • Is the solar permit finaled? Check the building permit for the solar installation. An open or failed permit is a problem, the system may not be properly connected or inspected.

How Solar Panels Affect Home Insurance

Solar panels add to your insurable value, they're part of the structure once installed. Your homeowners insurance needs to cover them. Leased panels can complicate claims because the solar company owns the equipment but you own the roof it's attached to. Make sure your insurance agent knows about the panels and whether they're owned or leased.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I remove leased solar panels if I don't want them?

Not without the solar company's permission, and usually not without paying an early termination fee or buying out the lease. The panels belong to them, and the lease is tied to the property. Removal without authorization can trigger breach of contract claims.

Do solar panels increase home value in Florida?

Owned panels generally do, studies show a 3-4% value increase on average. Leased panels are more complicated. Some buyers see them as a benefit (lower electric bills), while others see them as a liability (monthly payments, roof restrictions). The lease obligation can actually make the home harder to sell.

What if the seller says the panels are "paid off" but there's still a UCC filing?

The UCC filing may not have been terminated after the loan was paid. Ask for proof of payoff and then request a UCC-3 termination filing from the creditor. Don't close until the filing is cleared, otherwise, the lien follows the property.

title: Buyer Due Diligence Checklist for Tampa Bay Homes
excerpt: The complete due diligence checklist for buying a home in Tampa Bay, permits, taxes, CDD fees, solar liens, flood zones, insurance, and more.
content:
Quick Answer

What should I check before buying a home in Tampa Bay?

Pull the permit history, read the actual tax bill (check for CDD fees), search for solar liens, verify the flood zone, get an insurance quote before closing, and review HOA/CDD documents. This checklist covers every step.

Why Due Diligence Matters More in Florida

Florida real estate has layers that buyers from other states don't expect. CDD assessments that add thousands per year. Flood zones that require mandatory insurance. Wind mitigation requirements. HOAs with transfer fees and capital contributions. Solar panel leases with 20-year obligations. If you don't check these things before closing, you'll discover them on your first tax bill or insurance renewal, and by then, you own them.

I've been through this process hundreds of times with buyers across Tampa, Brandon, Valrico, Riverview, and all of Hillsborough County. This is the checklist I use for every transaction.

Step 1: Pull Permit History

Check what work has been done to the property and whether it was properly permitted and inspected. In Hillsborough County, use HillsGovHub for recent records and the older Building Permits Reports page for pre-2021 records.

What to look for: Open or expired permits, HVAC and roof permits (or lack thereof), unpermitted additions or conversions, missing final inspections.

Read the full guide: How to Check Permit History on a Hillsborough County Home

Step 2: Read the Actual Tax Bill

Don't rely on the listing's "estimated taxes", pull the real tax bill from hillstax.org. Look at every line item. The ad valorem section shows your regular property taxes. The non-ad-valorem section shows special assessments, including CDD fees, solid waste, stormwater, and any other district charges.

What to look for: CDD line items ($1,000-$4,000+/year), solid waste assessment amounts, any special assessment liens.

Read the full guide: How to Find CDD Fees Before Buying a Florida Home

Step 3: Check for Solar Panel Liens

If the home has solar panels, find out whether they're owned or leased. Search floridaucc.com for UCC filings under the homeowner's name. A UCC-1 filing mentioning solar or energy equipment means there's a lien.

What to look for: UCC-1 filings, solar lease terms, remaining balance, transfer requirements, roof warranty implications.

Read the full guide: How to Check for Solar Panel Liens

Have Questions About a Property You're Considering?

I'll pull the permits, check the tax bill, and flag anything you need to know before you make an offer.

Send Me the Address Call (813) 733-7907

Step 4: Verify the Flood Zone

Check the FEMA flood map at msc.fema.gov using the property address. Zone X means minimal flood risk (no mandatory flood insurance). Zones A, AE, AH, or V mean you're in a flood zone and flood insurance is required with a federally-backed mortgage.

Even in Zone X, consider flood insurance, Florida weather doesn't follow zone lines. But being in a mandatory flood zone adds $1,000-$5,000+ per year in insurance costs.

Step 5: Get an Insurance Quote Before Closing

Florida homeowners insurance is expensive and getting more so every year. Don't assume the seller's rate is what you'll pay, your premium depends on the home's age, roof condition, construction type, proximity to water, and your claims history. Get a quote from at least two or three carriers before you're under contract, not after. A home that looks affordable at the listing price may not be once you add a $6,000/year insurance bill.

Read more: Florida Homeowners Insurance Guide

Step 6: Review HOA and CDD Documents

If the property is in an HOA, request the full governing documents: bylaws, rules, financial statements, and meeting minutes. Look for pending special assessments, reserve fund health, and any pending litigation. For CDDs, request the district's annual budget and bond amortization schedule.

Key questions: What are the current dues? When was the last increase? Are there any pending special assessments? What's the reserve fund balance? Are there any lawsuits pending against the association?

Step 7: Title Search and Lien Check

Your title company handles this, but know what they're looking for: outstanding liens, judgments, unpaid taxes, mechanic's liens from contractors, and any encumbrances on the property. Title insurance protects you if something is missed, but a clean title search prevents most problems upfront.

Step 8: Home Inspection, But It's Not Enough Alone

A home inspection covers the physical condition of the property, roof, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, structure, appliances. It's essential, but it doesn't cover permits, taxes, liens, flood zones, or insurance. That's why this checklist exists, the inspection is one piece of the due diligence puzzle, not the whole thing.

Read more: Florida Home Inspection Guide

What I Check for Every Client

When you work with me, I handle steps 1 through 7 as part of the buying process. I pull permits, read tax bills, flag CDD fees, check flood zones, and coordinate with your lender and insurance agent to make sure there are no surprises. That's what 23+ years of experience looks like in practice, not just finding the house, but making sure the house is what it appears to be.

Barrett Henry | REMAX Collective
Direct: (813) 733-7907
Email: barrett@nowtb.com

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does due diligence take in Florida?

The inspection period in a Florida residential contract is typically 10 to 15 days. All of these checks should happen within that window. Permit and tax searches take minutes. Insurance quotes take 1-2 days. The home inspection itself takes 2-4 hours. I coordinate the timeline so nothing falls through the cracks.

Who pays for due diligence, the buyer or seller?

The buyer pays for the home inspection, insurance quotes, and any specialized inspections (termite, mold, etc.). Permit searches and tax bill reviews are free, they're public records. Title search costs are typically split or paid by the seller depending on the contract terms. HOA document fees are usually charged by the association ($150-$500).

What if I find a problem during due diligence?

That's exactly why you do it. Within the inspection period, you can negotiate repairs, request credits, ask the seller to resolve open permits, or walk away from the contract entirely. Finding problems after closing is expensive. Finding them before closing gives you leverage.

title: Buying a Florida Home With Solar Panels: Buyer Guide
excerpt: Owned vs leased, UCC liens, roof concerns, insurance impacts, and the 10 questions you must ask before buying a Florida home with solar panels.
content:
Quick Answer

What should I know before buying a home with solar panels in Florida?

The first question is whether the panels are owned or leased. Owned panels add value and convey free and clear. Leased panels come with a 20-25 year payment obligation, potential liens, and restrictions on your roof. Before making an offer, check the UCC filings, verify the building permit, and get the lease terms in writing.

Why solar changes the deal

Drive through Riverview, Wesley Chapel or Brandon and you will see panels on roof after roof. If you are house hunting in Tampa Bay you will encounter solar, and what you are really buying is a contract, a utility agreement, and a set of roof penetrations.

Solar can be a genuine asset: lower electric bills and, in some cases, better resale. It can also be a trap if you do not understand the ownership structure, the condition of the system, and the obligations that transfer to you at closing. Here is what I check for my buyers.

Owned vs. Leased, This Is the Whole Ballgame

There are fundamentally two situations, and they could not be more different:

Owned Solar PanelsLeased Solar Panels
Panels belong to the homeownerPanels belong to the solar company
No monthly payment to a solar companyMonthly lease payment ($100-$250/mo typical)
Convey with the home at sale, clean transferBuyer must qualify for and assume the lease
No UCC lien on the propertyUCC-1 filing (lien) on the equipment
Full control over roof repairs and replacementSolar company must coordinate any roof work
Adds 3-4% to home value on averageMay add value, may make home harder to sell
Warranty is with the buyerWarranty is with the solar company

If the panels are owned free and clear, congratulations, you're getting a bonus. The system generates electricity, reduces your FPL bill, and you have no ongoing obligation to anyone. The panels, inverter, and all equipment convey with the property like any other fixture.

If the panels are leased, you're inheriting a contract. A typical solar lease runs 20 to 25 years with monthly payments of $100 to $250. That's a $24,000 to $75,000 total obligation over the life of the lease. The solar company owns the equipment, and there's likely a UCC-1 financing statement filed with the state, which is essentially a lien. Read the full breakdown: How to Check for Solar Panel Liens

How to Verify Ownership Before Making an Offer

Step 1: Ask the Seller Directly

The listing agent should be able to tell you immediately whether the panels are owned or leased. If they can't answer or seem unsure, that's a yellow flag. Ask for documentation, the original purchase agreement, lease contract, or loan payoff statement.

Step 2: Search for UCC Filings

Go to floridaucc.com and run a debtor search under the seller's name. If a UCC-1 filing shows up mentioning solar, photovoltaic, or energy equipment, the panels are leased or financed. No filing usually means they're owned outright. This takes two minutes and costs nothing.

Step 3: Check the Building Permit

Every solar installation in Hillsborough County requires a building permit. Search HillsGovHub for a solar or photovoltaic permit on the property. The permit shows the contractor who installed the system, the date, and, critically, whether the final inspection passed. An open or failed solar permit means the system may not be properly connected to the grid.

Step 4: Review the Interconnection Agreement

The homeowner should have an interconnection agreement with the utility company (usually Duke Energy or Tampa Electric/TECO). This confirms the system is approved for net metering, meaning excess electricity generated by the panels flows back to the grid and creates credits on the electric bill. Without this agreement, the panels may be installed but not actually producing savings.

Considering a Home With Solar Panels?

I'll check the permit, pull the UCC filings, and tell you exactly what you're inheriting before you make an offer.

Send Me the Address Call (813) 733-7907

The 10 Questions You Must Ask Before Buying

  1. Are the panels owned, leased, or financed? Get documentation, not just a verbal answer.
  2. If leased: what are the monthly payments and how many years remain? Calculate the total remaining obligation.
  3. If leased: can the lease be transferred to a new buyer? Most can, but you'll need to qualify. What if you don't?
  4. If leased: what's the buyout price? Some leases allow early purchase. Get the number in writing.
  5. What is the system size (kW) and annual production (kWh)? This tells you how much electricity the panels actually generate.
  6. How old is the system? Solar panels degrade over time, typically 0.5-0.7% efficiency loss per year. A 10-year-old system produces less than a new one.
  7. What's the inverter warranty status? Inverters typically last 10-15 years and cost $1,500-$3,000 to replace. If the system is 12 years old, you may need a new inverter soon.
  8. Is the solar permit finaled? Open permits = uninspected work = potential problems.
  9. What happens if the roof needs replacement? Removing and reinstalling panels for a reroof costs $3,000-$10,000. Who pays if the panels are leased?
  10. Does the HOA have solar restrictions? Florida law (§163.04) protects homeowners' right to install solar, but some HOAs have placement and aesthetic requirements that could affect future modifications.

The insurance requirement that catches cash buyers

This is the one almost nobody knows about, and it bites cash buyers hardest.

If the system is large enough, your utility requires you to carry liability insurance as a condition of staying connected to the grid. Under Tampa Electric's standard interconnection agreement for Tier 2 renewable generator systems, a Tier 2 system is rated above 10 kW and no more than 100 kW alternating current, and the agreement states that the customer "shall maintain general liability insurance for personal injury and property damage in the amount of not less than one million dollars ($1,000,000)."

It is not a one-time form, either. The customer must provide initial proof of insurance and then submit proof of continuing coverage within 30 days of any policy renewal. Failure to maintain the required insurance is grounds for terminating the interconnection agreement, which means the system can be disconnected from the grid.

Why cash buyers get caught: a financed buyer has a lender requiring a homeowners policy, and the agent placing that policy usually catches the solar system and the liability requirement. A cash buyer has no lender forcing the conversation. I have seen cash buyers close, never file proof of coverage, and find out later that their interconnection is in default.

Two practical notes. First, dropping a Tier 2 system below 10 kW or pushing it above 100 kW requires a new agreement at a different tier, so changes to the array are not cosmetic. Second, systems above 100 kW up to 2 MW carry a higher requirement, not less than $2,000,000 in general liability. Confirm your system size in kW AC and your own utility's current tariff, because requirements differ by utility.

PACE assessments, and why they are different

Some Florida solar systems were financed through a PACE program, which stands for Property Assessed Clean Energy. This is not a loan in the normal sense. It is a non-ad valorem assessment attached to the property and collected on the property tax bill.

That distinction matters enormously:

  • It runs with the land, not the person. It does not get paid off because the owner moved. It transfers to you.
  • It can sit ahead of your mortgage in priority, which is exactly why many lenders require a PACE assessment to be paid off at closing before they will fund.
  • It shows up on the tax bill, not in a lien search for a mortgage. If you only look for a UCC filing or a recorded mortgage, you can miss it entirely.

Pull the property tax bill for the parcel and read the non-ad valorem assessment lines. If there is a PACE assessment, get the current payoff figure in writing and decide who pays it before you are at the closing table.

Getting the payoff handled at closing

If the panels are financed or leased with a buyout, the cleanest outcome is almost always a payoff at closing out of the seller's proceeds, with the lien released and the system conveyed to you free and clear. Make that an explicit term of the contract rather than an assumption.

What to require in writing:

  • A current payoff or buyout statement from the solar lender or lessor, with a good-through date.
  • Confirmation that the title company has the payoff in the closing figures and will obtain a release or UCC termination.
  • If instead you are assuming a lease or power purchase agreement, the lessor's written approval of you as the transferee, completed before your inspection period ends. Transfer approval is not automatic and it is not fast.

The failure mode here is predictable: everyone assumes the lease transfer is a formality, nobody starts the paperwork, and the closing gets delayed while the solar company runs a credit check on the buyer.

Roof penetration warranties

A solar array is bolted through your roof covering. Every mount is a hole that was flashed and sealed by the solar installer, not by the roofer.

That creates a split responsibility that matters the first time water shows up in a ceiling:

  • Ask whether the roofing manufacturer's warranty was voided by the installation. Some manufacturers void coverage unless the array was installed by a certified installer using approved mounts.
  • Ask for the installer's separate penetration or weatherproofing warranty, its term, and whether it transfers to a new owner. Many are 5 or 10 years and many do not transfer.
  • Get both warranty documents before your inspection period ends. A leak around a mount with no transferable warranty and a voided roof warranty is entirely your cost.

Also have your inspector look at the attic directly beneath the array. Staining on the sheathing tells you more than a visual roof inspection from the ground.

While you are inspecting an older Florida home, order the insurance inspections at the same time. My guide to what fails a Florida 4-point inspection covers how roof age interacts with insurability, which is the other half of this problem.

How Solar Panels Affect Your Home Insurance

Solar panels are attached to the structure, so they become part of your insurable property. Your homeowners insurance policy needs to cover the replacement cost of the panels, typically $15,000 to $30,000 for a residential system. If you don't update your coverage, you could be underinsured.

Leased panels add a wrinkle: the solar company owns the equipment, but it's on your roof. If a hurricane damages the panels, who files the claim? Typically, the solar company has their own insurance on the equipment, but your policy covers the roof damage underneath. Get clarity on this before closing, not during a storm.

Some insurance carriers charge higher premiums for homes with solar panels because of the increased replacement cost and the complexity of roof claims. Shop around and get quotes from at least three carriers.

How Solar Panels Affect the Home's Value

Studies from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory show that owned solar panels increase home value by an average of $15,000 to $20,000 (roughly 3-4%). However, that premium depends on the local market, the system's age, and whether it's owned or leased.

Owned systems almost always add value. Buyers see reduced electric bills with no strings attached.

Leased systems are more complicated. Some buyers view the lease payment as a wash, you're paying $150/month for the lease but saving $150/month on electricity. Others see it as a liability, a 15-year obligation they didn't ask for, plus restrictions on roof work. In my experience, leased panels neither add nor subtract significant value, but they do narrow your buyer pool at resale because some buyers simply won't take on the lease.

Roof Condition and Solar, The Hidden Cost

Here's something most buyers don't think about: what's the age of the roof under those panels?

If the roof is 15 years old and the solar panels were installed 5 years ago, you may need a new roof in the next 5-10 years. That means removing all the panels, replacing the roof, and reinstalling the panels. The removal and reinstallation alone costs $3,000-$10,000 depending on the system size and type.

If the panels are leased, the solar company typically handles the removal and reinstallation, but they charge for it, and the scheduling can delay your reroof by weeks. If the panels are owned, you're coordinating with a solar installer separately from your roofer.

Before you buy: check the roof permit history. When was the last reroof? What's the remaining useful life? Factor the cost of panel removal/reinstallation into your long-term ownership budget.

Net Metering in Florida, What You're Actually Getting

Florida's net metering program allows solar homeowners to send excess electricity back to the grid and receive credits on their utility bill. This is what makes solar financially viable for most homeowners, the panels generate more electricity during peak sun hours than the home uses, and that excess offsets nighttime and cloudy-day usage.

As a buyer, ask for 12 months of the seller's electric bills. This shows you the actual savings the system produces, not the theoretical production, but real-world results accounting for the home's usage patterns, the system's age, and seasonal variation. If the seller claims "zero electric bills" but the bills show $80/month credits, you know the real picture.

The Due Diligence Checklist for Homes With Solar

Use this alongside the full buyer due diligence checklist:

  • Confirm owned vs. leased (get documentation)
  • Search floridaucc.com for UCC-1 filings
  • Pull the solar building permit, verify it's finaled
  • Get the interconnection agreement with the utility
  • Request 12 months of electric bills
  • Check system age and inverter warranty
  • Assess roof age and condition under the panels
  • Get insurance quotes that include the solar system
  • If leased: get the full lease document, remaining term, monthly payment, buyout price, and transfer requirements
  • If leased: confirm the lease transfer with the solar company before removing your inspection contingency

Considering a Home With Solar Panels?

I'll check the permit, pull the UCC filings, and tell you exactly what you're inheriting before you make an offer.

Send Me the Address Call (813) 733-7907

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I avoid buying a home with leased solar panels?

Not necessarily, but go in with your eyes open. If the lease payment is reasonable, the system is generating real savings, and the transfer process is straightforward, a leased system can work fine. The problem is when buyers don't discover the lease terms until they're already under contract. Know the full picture upfront and factor the lease payment into your monthly budget alongside CDD fees, HOA dues, insurance, and taxes.

Can a seller remove solar panels before selling?

If they own the panels, yes, but it's unusual. Removing panels means patching the roof where the mounts were, which adds cost. If the panels are leased, the seller would need to buy out the lease first, which can cost $10,000-$20,000 depending on the remaining term. Most sellers prefer to transfer the system rather than remove it.

Do solar panels void the roof warranty?

They shouldn't if installed properly by a licensed contractor. However, if the installation damaged the roof or wasn't permitted, the roofing manufacturer may deny warranty claims on the affected area. Check the original roof warranty and the solar installation permit to make sure everything was done by the book.

How do I know if the solar system is actually working?

Most modern systems have monitoring apps (Tesla, Enphase, SolarEdge) that show real-time production data. Ask the seller to share monitoring access so you can see the system's actual output. If there's no monitoring or the seller can't show production data, that's a concern, the system may be underperforming or partially non-functional.

What if the solar company goes out of business?

If you own the panels, the warranty may be difficult to enforce but the panels continue working. If you lease, a bankrupt solar company creates a messy situation, you may still owe payments on a lease that no one is servicing. This has happened with several smaller solar companies in Florida. It's one more reason to verify the financial stability of the solar company if you're assuming a lease.

Sources

  • Tampa Electric Standard Interconnection Agreement for Tier 2 Renewable Generator Systems (10 kW to 100 kW AC definition, $1,000,000 general liability requirement, renewal proof, termination for lapse)
  • Fla. Admin. Code R. 25-6.065 (Florida Public Service Commission net metering and interconnection for investor-owned utilities)
  • Fla. Stat. 163.08 (PACE, qualifying improvements financed by non-ad valorem assessment)
  • Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, Inspections (roof and 4-point requirements)

title: Selling a Home With Solar Panels in Florida: The Complete Seller's Guide
excerpt: How to sell a Florida home with solar panels, whether owned or leased. Pricing strategy, disclosure requirements, lease transfers, and how to make solar a selling point.
content:
Quick Answer

How do I sell a home with solar panels in Florida?

If you own the panels, highlight the energy savings in your listing, owned solar adds 3-4% to home value. If you lease, start the lease transfer process early, disclose the terms upfront, and consider a lease buyout if the numbers make sense. Either way, have the system documentation, permit records, and electric bills ready for buyers.

Selling With Owned Solar Panels

If you own your solar panels outright, paid cash or paid off the loan, you're in a strong position. Owned solar is a genuine selling feature. Studies from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory show homes with owned solar sell for 3-4% more than comparable homes without panels.

Here's how to maximize the value:

  • Get your documentation together. Buyers will ask for proof of ownership (purchase agreement or loan payoff statement), the original building permit, the interconnection agreement with the utility, and the manufacturer's warranty documentation.
  • Show the savings. Pull 12 months of electric bills showing the actual reduction. If your monthly bill went from $250 to $40, that's $2,500/year in savings, a compelling selling point.
  • Highlight the system specs in the listing. System size (kW), annual production (kWh), brand, age, and remaining warranty. Buyers shopping for solar homes want these details.
  • Make sure the permit is finaled. An open solar permit will spook buyers and their agents. If yours isn't closed out, check the permit status and get it resolved before listing.

Selling With a Leased Solar System

Leased panels are trickier but absolutely manageable if you plan ahead. The key is transparency and preparation.

Option 1: Transfer the Lease to the Buyer

Most solar leases allow transfer to a new homeowner. The buyer needs to qualify with the solar company (credit check), and then the lease obligation transfers at closing. Start this process as soon as you list, it can take 2-4 weeks for the solar company to process the transfer.

What to prepare:

  • Full copy of the lease agreement
  • Remaining term and monthly payment amount
  • Transfer requirements from the solar company
  • Contact info for the solar company's transfer department

Option 2: Buy Out the Lease Before Selling

If the buyout price is reasonable and your home's value supports it, paying off the lease and converting to owned panels can be smart. You'll sell with owned solar (which adds value) instead of a lease obligation (which some buyers resist). Get the buyout quote from the solar company and compare it to the expected value bump.

Option 3: Offer to Pay the Lease Off as a Seller Concession

If a buyer wants the home but not the lease, you can offer to buy out the lease as part of the negotiation, essentially rolling it into the deal. This can be more effective than a price reduction because it eliminates the buyer's objection entirely.

Selling a Home With Solar? Let's Talk Strategy.

I'll help you position the solar system as a selling point, or navigate the lease transfer if needed.

Get a Free Valuation Call (813) 733-7907

Florida Disclosure Requirements for Solar

Florida law requires sellers to disclose material facts about the property. A solar lease is absolutely a material fact, it's a financial obligation that transfers with the property. You must disclose:

  • Whether the panels are owned or leased
  • The terms of any lease or power purchase agreement (PPA)
  • Any UCC filings on the equipment
  • The condition and age of the system
  • Any known issues with the system's performance

Failing to disclose a solar lease can lead to post-closing disputes, rescission claims, or lawsuits. Be upfront, it's both the legal requirement and the smart strategy.

How to Price a Home With Solar

Owned solar: Price your home at the top of the comparable range and use the solar system as justification. If similar homes without solar are selling for $400K, you can reasonably list at $412K-$416K (the 3-4% premium).

Leased solar: Price competitively with comparable homes without solar. The lease payment roughly offsets the energy savings, so the net impact on value is close to zero. Don't try to charge a premium for leased panels, sophisticated buyers will see through it. Instead, position the lease as a benefit: "Solar panels reduce your electric bill to an average of $X/month."

For a current valuation, request a free home valuation I'll factor in the solar system's impact on your specific market.

Common Mistakes Sellers Make

  1. Not disclosing the lease. This is the biggest one. Some sellers or listing agents try to downplay or ignore the lease, hoping buyers won't ask. They will. And if they don't, their agent, lender, or title company will. Disclose proactively.
  2. Starting the transfer process too late. Solar company transfer departments are not fast. Start the process when you list, not when you're under contract. A delayed transfer can blow up a closing timeline.
  3. Not having documentation ready. Buyers want to see the lease agreement, electric bills, production data, warranty info, and permit status. Having this organized and available from day one makes your listing more professional and reduces friction during due diligence.
  4. Overpricing based on the solar investment. What you paid for the system is not what it adds to the home's value. A $30,000 system doesn't add $30,000 to the sale price, especially if it's 10 years old. Price based on market comparables and the actual value premium solar commands in your neighborhood.
  5. Ignoring the roof condition. Buyers will ask about the roof age under the panels. If the roof is 18 years old, they're factoring in a $15,000-$25,000 reroof plus $5,000-$10,000 for panel removal and reinstallation. That's a $20K-$35K future cost that affects what they'll offer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do solar panels make a home harder to sell?

Owned panels typically make homes easier to sell, they're a feature buyers want. Leased panels can narrow your buyer pool slightly because some buyers don't want to assume the lease. However, most leases are transferable, and the energy savings offset the payment. Proper disclosure and preparation prevent most friction.

Can a buyer refuse to assume my solar lease?

Yes, and this is why you need a backup plan. If the buyer won't assume the lease, you can offer to buy it out, negotiate a seller concession, or find a different buyer. Having the buyout price ready gives you options. Most solar companies will also allow the seller to prepay the remaining lease if the buyer objects.

Should I remove the solar panels before selling?

Almost never. Removal costs $3,000-$8,000, you'll need to patch the roof, and you lose the selling feature entirely. The only scenario where removal makes sense is if the system is non-functional, unpermitted, or the lease terms are so unfavorable that no buyer will accept them and the buyout cost exceeds the system's value.

How do I find out what my solar system is worth?

For owned systems, appraisers use the income approach (projected energy savings over remaining life) or the cost approach (depreciated replacement cost). The Appraisal Institute's residential green energy addendum is the standard method. As a rough estimate, deduct 0.5-0.7% efficiency per year from installation, and value the remaining production at current electricity rates.

title: How to Transfer a Solar Lease When Selling Your Florida Home
excerpt: Step-by-step guide to transferring a solar lease to your buyer in Florida, timeline, requirements, what to do if the buyer won't qualify, and buyout options.
content:
Quick Answer

How do I transfer a solar lease when selling my home?

Contact your solar company's transfer department as soon as you list. The buyer will need to apply and pass a credit check. Most transfers take 2-4 weeks. Start early, a delayed transfer is one of the most common reasons solar-related closings get pushed back.

The Solar Lease Transfer Timeline

Most sellers underestimate how long this takes. Here's the realistic timeline:

  1. Week 1: Contact your solar company when you list. Get the transfer packet, current balance, buyout quote, and list of requirements for the new buyer.
  2. Week 2-3 (under contract): Provide the buyer with the lease agreement and transfer packet. The buyer submits their application and credit information to the solar company.
  3. Week 3-4: Solar company reviews the application, runs credit, and issues approval or denial. If approved, they prepare the transfer documents.
  4. Closing: Transfer documents are signed at closing alongside the deed and mortgage paperwork.

If the solar company is slow (and some are), this can take 4-6 weeks. That's why starting before you're under contract is critical.

What the Buyer Needs to Qualify

Solar companies treat the lease transfer like a new credit application. The buyer typically needs:

  • Minimum credit score (usually 650-700 depending on the company)
  • Proof of income or employment
  • Proof of homeownership (the purchase contract)
  • Agreement to the existing lease terms

If the buyer doesn't qualify, you have three options: negotiate a lease buyout as part of the sale, find a co-signer (rare), or accept that this particular buyer can't purchase the home with the lease intact and adjust accordingly.

Selling a Home With Solar? Let's Talk Strategy.

I'll help you position the solar system as a selling point, or navigate the lease transfer if needed.

Get a Free Valuation Call (813) 733-7907

What If the Buyer Won't Take the Lease?

This happens. Some buyers want the house but refuse to assume a 15-year solar obligation. Your options:

  • Buy out the lease. Get the payoff quote from the solar company. If it's $12,000 and your home is priced right, this may be worth doing to close the deal. You can build the cost into the sale price or absorb it.
  • Offer a seller credit. Offer the buyer a closing credit equal to 1-2 years of lease payments. This sweetens the deal without you eating the entire buyout cost.
  • Prepay the lease. Some companies allow you to prepay the remaining lease in a lump sum, converting the panels to "owned" status for the buyer. This is effectively a buyout but through a different mechanism.
  • Walk away and find another buyer. If the numbers don't work with this buyer, wait for one who sees the solar as a feature rather than a burden.

Solar Companies and Their Transfer Processes

Every solar company handles transfers differently. Here are the major players in Florida:

  • Sunrun: Has a dedicated transfer team. Process typically takes 3-4 weeks. Credit requirement around 650.
  • Tesla/SolarCity: Transfer through Tesla's energy division. Can be slower, budget 4-6 weeks. Online portal available.
  • Vivint Solar (now Sunrun): Merged with Sunrun. Contact Sunrun's transfer department for legacy Vivint leases.
  • Sunnova: Transfer process is straightforward but can take 3-4 weeks. Credit requirement around 680.
  • Local installers: Varies widely. Some are very responsive, others are hard to reach. Start early and follow up aggressively.

Documents You Need Ready

  • Original solar lease or PPA agreement
  • Current monthly payment amount and remaining term
  • Buyout/payoff quote from the solar company
  • Transfer application packet
  • Solar building permit (verify it's finaled)
  • 12 months of electric bills showing savings
  • System monitoring data (production reports)
  • Manufacturer warranty documentation

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell my home if the solar company won't approve the transfer?

Yes, but you'll likely need to buy out the lease first. If the solar company denies the buyer's transfer application, the lease stays with you, and you can't sell the home with a lease obligation that has no qualified assignee. The buyout removes the obstacle entirely.

Who pays for the lease transfer?

Most solar companies don't charge a transfer fee. However, some charge $200-$500 for administrative processing. Check your lease agreement for transfer fee provisions. In most deals, the seller covers any transfer costs.

Does a solar lease affect my ability to get a clear title?

A UCC-1 filing associated with a solar lease will appear in the title search. It's not a title defect, it's a disclosed encumbrance. But the title company will require the lease transfer or payoff to be handled at closing to ensure clean title passes to the buyer. This is routine, not a problem, as long as you start the process early enough.

Homes for sale in Gibsonton FL range from $220K to $500K+, with most buyers finding 3-bedroom, 2-bath concrete block homes in the $280K-$390K range. Gibsonton (ZIP 33534) sits in southern Hillsborough County along the Alafia River, offering lower purchase prices than neighboring Riverview while sharing the same I-75 access. No HOA or CDD fees apply to most Gibsonton addresses, which meaningfully lowers your monthly carrying cost compared to newer suburban communities.

What Types of Homes Are for Sale in Gibsonton FL?

Gibsonton's housing stock is overwhelmingly concrete block single-family homes built between the 1960s and early 2000s. A smaller pocket of newer construction sits along the community's northern fringe near Riverview. Townhomes and condos are rare here. Most buyers are choosing between older resale homes that need updating and move-in-ready mid-2000s construction.

Entry-Level: $220K-$290K

At this price point you are typically looking at 2-3 bedroom, 1-2 bath homes built in the 1960s through 1980s. Expect original kitchens, single-pane windows, older plumbing, and roof systems that may be 15-20 years old. These homes tend to be 900-1,400 sq ft on modest lots. They can be excellent values if you budget for updates, but a thorough inspection is essential. The most important items to evaluate: roof age, electrical panel (some older homes still have Federal Pacific or Zinsco panels), plumbing material (galvanized vs copper vs PVC), and HVAC age.

Mid-Range: $290K-$390K

This is the core of the Gibsonton market. Homes here are typically 3-4 bedrooms, 2 baths, 1,400-2,200 sq ft, built in the late 1980s through early 2000s. Most are in good condition with updated roofs and HVAC systems. Many have one-car or two-car garages, fenced yards, and are move-in ready. Communities like Carriage Pointe and Kings Lake fall in this tier. Some sections of Carriage Pointe have an HOA (around $200-$600/year); Kings Lake is mostly HOA-free.

Upper Range: $390K-$500K+

Larger homes (2,200-3,200 sq ft), corner lots, and waterfront properties along or near the Alafia River push into this tier. A limited number of 4-5 bedroom homes with newer construction (2010s) also compete here. Alafia River frontage adds significant premium and introduces flood zone requirements. Verify flood zone status at msc.fema.gov before making any offer on a Gibsonton waterfront or near-water property.

Carriage Pointe is one of Gibsonton's larger planned subdivisions, built primarily in the early 2000s. Homes are typically 3-5 bedrooms, 1,600-3,200 sq ft, and are priced between $310K-$460K. Kings Lake

Kings Lake is a smaller neighborhood of mostly 1980s-1990s ranch-style homes on modest lots without HOA fees. Prices generally run $260K-$360K. It sits centrally in the 33534 ZIP code along Gibsonton Drive. The absence of HOA makes it popular with buyers who want flexibility on use of their property.

SilverStone

SilverStone is a gated community in the Gibsonton area with newer-era construction, typically 3-4 bedrooms in the $340K-$480K range. The gated entry and planned community layout attract buyers who want more suburban structure while still benefiting from Gibsonton's lower overall price levels.

Older Gibsonton Core

The older portions of Gibsonton along US-41 and the streets north and south of Gibsonton Drive include the most affordable housing in the 33534 ZIP. These are primarily 1960s-1980s CBS homes with no HOA and lower square footage. Values here have risen sharply since 2020 but remain accessible for buyers who need to stay under $300K in Hillsborough County.

Most Gibsonton homes sell in the $280K-$420K range, which puts them solidly in conventional financing territory. VA and FHA loans are fully applicable here. USDA Rural Development does not apply because Gibsonton is not designated as a rural area. Get pre-approved with at least 2-3 lenders and compare rates and fees, not just the headline rate.

Step 2: Flood Zone Check First

Before falling in love with any Gibsonton listing, run the address through FEMA's Flood Map Service Center at msc.fema.gov. Properties in Zone AE (the Alafia River corridor and some canal-adjacent streets) require flood insurance that can add $1,500-$5,000+/year to your carrying cost. This is a deciding factor for many buyers, not an afterthought.

Step 3: Inspect Everything

On older Gibsonton homes (pre-1990), pay particular attention to the 4-point inspection components: roof, electrical, HVAC, and plumbing. Florida insurance carriers require a 4-point inspection for homes over 25 years old. If the roof is nearing 15 years, budget for a near-term replacement ($10K-$20K range). If you see an older Federal Pacific or Zinsco electrical panel, factor in panel replacement ($2,500-$4,500).

Gibsonton homeowners insurance runs approximately $2,200-$3,800/year for non-flood-zone properties depending on home age, roof material, and distance to fire station. title: Gibsonton FL Schools: East Bay High, Giunta Middle & Elementary
excerpt: Complete guide to schools serving Gibsonton, FL, elementary through high school ratings, zoning, and how school choice affects home values.
content:
Quick Answer: Gibsonton FL Schools (ZIP 33534)

Most Gibsonton addresses zone to Gibsonton Elementary or Corr Elementary (K-5), Giunta Middle School (6-8), and East Bay High School (9-12), all part of Hillsborough County Public Schools. East Bay High is a strong traditional school with CTE and JROTC but ranks below Hillsborough's top academic performers. Families seeking higher AP pass rates can apply for school choice and magnet programs through HCPS. Always verify your exact address assignment at hcpss.org before purchasing.

For buyers with school-age children, the school zone is often as important as the home itself. Gibsonton FL (ZIP 33534) is served entirely by Hillsborough County Public Schools (HCPS), the eighth-largest school district in the United States. Here is a complete picture of what the 33534 zone offers, how it compares to nearby communities, and what your options are if you want something different.

What Schools Serve Gibsonton FL?

Elementary Schools: Gibsonton Elementary and Corr Elementary

Gibsonton Elementary School (K-5) is the primary elementary school for most 33534 addresses. The school offers a standard Hillsborough County curriculum with emphasis on literacy and math foundations. Class sizes align with Florida's class size requirements. The school has a relatively small enrollment compared to many Hillsborough County elementaries, which can mean a more community-oriented feel. A portion of western Gibsonton addresses zone to Corr Elementary School instead. Both schools participate in HCPS's standard assessment and accountability system.

Florida assigns schools letter grades (A through F) annually based on standardized test performance, learning gains, and other metrics. These grades change from year to year. Check fldoe.org for the current grade before making a purchasing decision based on school rating alone. A single year's grade does not tell the complete story of a school's quality or community culture.

Middle School: Giunta Middle School (Grades 6-8)

Giunta Middle School serves Gibsonton and portions of Riverview. The school offers Hillsborough's standard middle school curriculum with honors and advanced tracks, electives covering performing arts, technology, and physical education, and a range of extracurricular clubs. Dual enrollment opportunities are not typically offered at the middle school level, but gifted and advanced coursework is available for qualifying students.

Giunta has shown improving performance on state assessments in recent years. Students who wish to attend a magnet middle school elsewhere in the county may apply during the annual school choice window. Transportation is not guaranteed for magnet placements far from 33534.

High School: East Bay High School (Grades 9-12)

East Bay High School (9-12) is the assigned high school for most Gibsonton (33534) residents. East Bay is a comprehensive high school with a total enrollment of approximately 2,200-2,600 students. The school offers:

  • Standard diploma and advanced diploma tracks
  • Advanced Placement (AP) courses across core subjects
  • Career and Technical Education (CTE) programs including health science, automotive, and construction trades
  • Junior ROTC (Air Force and Army programs)
  • Dual enrollment through Hillsborough Community College (HCC)
  • Active athletics across 20+ varsity sports
  • Performing arts, marching band, and clubs

AP course participation and passing rates at East Bay are below Hillsborough's top-tier high schools (Plant, Newsome, Steinbrenner, Gaither). East Bay's strength is in its CTE pathways and vocational programs rather than college prep rankings. Graduation rates are comparable to the county average. For families whose primary concern is AP performance and college placement statistics, school choice options are worth exploring.
