Redington Beach can work for both short-term and long-term rental investors, but with caveats. Pinellas County requires STR registration. For long-term rental, demand is steady from retirees and Gulf beach lifestyle seekers. Flood insurance and insurance costs generally are the primary investment risk variable.

Is Redington Beach FL in a flood zone?

Yes. Virtually all of Redington Beach is in a FEMA flood zone. Gulf-front properties are typically Zone VE (wave velocity action), which carries the highest insurance costs. Intracoastal, canal-front, and interior properties are typically Zone AE. Very few properties in Redington Beach are in Zone X. Flood insurance is required for all financed properties in Zones VE and AE.

Does Redington Beach have HOA fees or CDD fees?

Single-family homes in Redington Beach generally do not have HOA fees, the town itself is a small barrier island community without homeowner associations governing most SFH lots. Condominiums have HOA fees that vary widely by building, typically $400-$2,000+/month depending on building size, amenities, and current reserve funding status under SB 4-D requirements. There are no CDD (Community Development District) fees in Redington Beach.

Florida's property tax system is one of the first topics I walk buyers through when they start looking in Redington Beach. How Are Redington Beach FL Property Taxes Calculated?

Florida property taxes are calculated by multiplying the taxable value of a property by the combined millage rate. The taxable value is the assessed value minus any applicable exemptions (homestead, senior, veteran, disability). Millage rates are expressed as dollars per $1,000 of taxable value, so a 20-mill rate means $20 per $1,000, or 2%.

For high-value properties, homestead saves the same dollar amount as it does for lower-value properties, it is not proportional. Portability (see below) provides additional tax savings for buyers coming from another Florida homesteaded property.

Florida Homestead Exemption: How It Works in Redington Beach

The Florida homestead exemption provides up to $50,000 reduction in taxable value for your primary residence:

First $25,000, applies to all taxing authorities including school board. Second $25,000 (value between $50,000-$75,000 of assessed value), applies to non-school millage only. Combined, these two exemptions save Redington Beach homeowners approximately $3,000-$3,600/year at typical millage rates.

To claim homestead exemption, you must: be a Florida resident, use the property as your primary residence, and have owned the property as of January 1 of the tax year. Apply online or in person at pcpao.gov or at 315 Court St., Clearwater, FL 33756, (727) 464-3207, by March 1.

The Save Our Homes Cap: Critical Information for Buyers

The Save Our Homes (SOH) amendment limits annual increases in a homesteaded property's assessed value to the lesser of 3% or the CPI. This benefit compounds over time, a property bought in 2000 for $200,000 might have a current market value of $1,200,000 but a SOH-capped assessed value of $400,000, meaning the current owner pays taxes on only $400,000, not $1,200,000.

When that property sells, the SOH cap resets to zero. The new buyer's first assessed value will be based on the sale price (market value). This is one of the most important facts for buyers in Redington Beach, where properties have often been held for many years with dramatically compressed SOH assessments. Always use the new assessed value (approximately equal to purchase price) when projecting your post-closing tax bill, not the current owner's tax bill.

Florida Homestead Portability: How to Save on Taxes When Moving to Redington Beach

If you are buying in Redington Beach and are leaving another Florida homesteaded property, portability allows you to transfer your accumulated SOH benefit to your new home. This can reduce your taxable value significantly in year one.

Portability rules: Maximum transfer is $500,000 of SOH benefit. You must apply within 3 years of abandoning your prior Florida homestead. File Form DR-501T at pcpao.gov with your homestead application. The benefit is calculated based on the ratio of your prior home's SOH benefit to its assessed value, applied proportionally to your new home.

Step 5: To estimate your post-purchase taxes, use the market value (purchase price) as your estimated new assessed value and apply the current total millage rate.

Quick Answer: There is no vacant land for traditional new construction in Redington Beach FL. The barrier island is fully built out. The only path to new construction is teardown-rebuild, buying an existing home, demolishing it, and building new. Gulf-front teardown-rebuilds run $1.5M-$4M+ all-in. Redington Beach FL New Construction: Teardown-Rebuild Guide, Costs, and FEMA Requirements

If you want a brand-new home in Redington Beach, you need to understand one fundamental fact: there is no vacant land left. Redington Beach is a narrow barrier island that was fully developed decades ago. Every buildable lot has a structure on it. The only way to get new construction here is to buy an existing home, demolish it, and build new in its place, a process commonly called teardown-rebuild or infill construction. I have worked with buyers who are interested in this path, and I am honest with them upfront: it is complex, expensive, time-consuming, and requires navigating both Pinellas County permitting and FEMA flood zone compliance. If that sounds right for your project, here is what you need to know.

Why Is There No New Construction in Redington Beach FL?

Redington Beach is a narrow barrier island between the Gulf of Mexico and Boca Ciega Bay. The town covers approximately 0.3 square miles of land area, less than half a square mile. It was incorporated in 1940 and was substantially developed by the 1970s and 1980s. Every lot that could be built on was built on long ago. There is no municipal or county land set aside for new development, and no large undeveloped tracts exist anywhere on the island.

This is actually one of Redington Beach's characteristics that attracts a certain buyer, no new construction means no construction activity, no builders' trucks, no staged model homes. The neighborhood is stable and quiet. But it also means that if you want a newly constructed home specifically in Redington Beach, teardown-rebuild is your only option.

These are broad ranges. The actual cost depends on the lot size, water frontage, design complexity, material choices, and the specific builder you select. Get detailed cost estimates from at least three licensed Florida contractors before committing to a project.

FEMA Flood Zone Requirements for New Construction in Redington Beach

Zone VE (Gulf-Front) Construction Requirements

Zone VE is the highest-risk and most regulated flood zone. It designates areas subject to wave action in addition to flooding. For new construction in Zone VE, the requirements are:

Lowest floor must be elevated above the Base Flood Elevation (BFE) plus any local freeboard requirement (Pinellas County may require 1-2 feet of freeboard above BFE). The structure must be built on an open foundation, piers, columns, or pilings. No enclosed space is permitted below the BFE, the space below the elevated floor must be open or enclosed only with non-load-bearing breakaway walls. This means no garage, no enclosed storage, no living space below BFE. HVAC equipment must be above BFE. Utilities (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) must be elevated above BFE or protected with flood-resistant materials.

These requirements significantly affect the design and cost of Gulf-front construction. The open-pile foundation and elevated first floor create a distinct architectural look, typical Gulf-front homes sit 8-16+ feet off the ground on pilings, with parking, storage, and utility space below.

Zone AE (Canal-Front and Interior) Construction Requirements

Zone AE requires the lowest floor to be at or above the Base Flood Elevation. Unlike Zone VE, enclosed construction below BFE is permitted in Zone AE, but if enclosed space is below BFE it must have flood openings (vents or engineered flood openings) to equalize water pressure and does not count as living space. Many builders in AE zones elevate the first floor 1-2 feet above BFE (freeboard) to reduce flood insurance premiums significantly.

FDEP Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL) Permits

Gulf-front properties in Redington Beach fall seaward of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL). Any new construction, substantial improvement, or major alteration seaward of the CCCL requires a FDEP permit in addition to Pinellas County building permits.

The CCCL permitting process through FDEP Bureau of Beaches and Coastal Systems typically takes 3-6 months for review and approval. Complex projects or those involving dune systems may take longer. FDEP permits include conditions related to setbacks from the shoreline, vegetation management, and design standards. Contact FDEP at myfloridaenvironment.com or (850) 245-2094 for guidance specific to your project.

This includes the existing home purchase price, demolition ($15,000-$35,000+), engineering and architecture ($40,000-$120,000+), permitting fees, elevated foundation construction ($60,000-$180,000+), and construction at $350-$600+/square foot. Total timelines typically run 24-36 months from purchase to completion.

What FEMA requirements apply to new construction in Redington Beach FL?

All new construction in Redington Beach must comply with FEMA flood zone regulations. For Zone VE (Gulf-front), the lowest floor must be elevated above the Base Flood Elevation (BFE) plus any local freeboard requirement, and no enclosed living space is permitted below BFE, only open lattice or breakaway walls. For Zone AE (interior and canal-front), elevated construction on piers, columns, or fill is required with the lowest floor at or above BFE. These requirements are enforced through Pinellas County building permits.

Do I need a FDEP CCCL permit to build in Redington Beach?

Gulf-front properties in Redington Beach fall within the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL). Any construction seaward of the CCCL requires a FDEP permit in addition to Pinellas County building permits. FDEP CCCL permits typically take 3-6 months for review and approval, adding significant time to the build process. Contact FDEP at myfloridaenvironment.com for current requirements.

Are there new construction alternatives near Redington Beach FL?

Yes. Buyers who want new construction at a lower cost point can find it on the mainland Pinellas County or Hillsborough County communities within 30-50 miles. Communities like Largo, Clearwater, Dunedin, and Wesley Chapel have infill new construction and new developments. These are significantly less expensive per square foot and do not carry the Zone VE open-pile foundation requirements, but they do not have the Gulf barrier island location.

Florida DBPR Vacation Rental License

Condo HOA Rental Restrictions (Critical)

Before making an offer on any condo for investment purposes, request the full Declaration of Condominium (not just the bylaws or rules and regulations, the Declaration is the controlling document) and have it reviewed by a Florida real estate attorney. This is a non-negotiable due diligence step.

Redington Beach has two kinds of waterfront, and understanding the difference matters before you make an offer. Gulf-front homes face the Gulf of Mexico directly, you walk out the back door to the beach. Gulf-Front Properties in Redington Beach FL

Gulf-front properties in Redington Beach sit directly on the Gulf of Mexico. The western shoreline of the island faces open water with some natural beach, sea oats, and dune areas. Gulf-front homes offer the most desirable lifestyle in Redington Beach, direct beach access, Gulf sunsets viewed from your back porch, and the sound of waves.

The tradeoffs are real: Gulf-front properties are in Zone VE, which has the highest flood insurance costs and the most restrictive building requirements. Zone VE indicates a velocity zone, meaning the property is subject not only to flooding but to wave action and storm surge force. Insurance carriers treat VE zone properties as high-risk, and NFIP policies for VE zone structures often hit the maximum coverage limit of $250,000 for the building, requiring supplemental private flood insurance for high-value homes.

Canal-front homes with docks provide boat access to the Gulf of Mexico via Johns Pass, approximately 2-3 miles south of Redington Beach along the Intracoastal Waterway. Johns Pass is a natural pass between Madeira Beach and Treasure Island that connects the Intracoastal to the Gulf. Traveling by boat from a Redington Beach canal dock to the open Gulf via Johns Pass typically takes 20-35 minutes depending on water traffic and no-wake zones.

The Intracoastal in this area is popular for kayaking, paddleboarding, fishing (redfish, snook, sea trout, mangrove snapper), and dolphin/manatee watching. Dolphins are regularly observed in Boca Ciega Bay adjacent to Redington Beach.

Elevation Certificate: Why You Need One Before Closing

An elevation certificate (EC) is a document prepared by a licensed land surveyor that certifies the elevation of the lowest floor of a building relative to the Base Flood Elevation (BFE). Canal-front and interior properties are Zone AE ($1.5K-$8K+/yr). Flood insurance is required for all financed properties. Redington Beach is Pinellas County Evacuation Zone A, mandatory evacuation for major hurricanes.

Redington Beach FL Flood Zones: Zone VE, Zone AE, Insurance Costs, and What Buyers Need to Know

Every buyer I work with in Redington Beach gets the same briefing early in the process: this is a barrier island, and essentially every property on this island is in a flood zone. That is not a dealbreaker, it is a fact of Gulf Coast barrier island living that needs to be budgeted accurately. The flood zone determines your insurance costs, your construction requirements, and your storm evacuation obligations. Buyers who understand this upfront make better decisions than those who find out at closing that their annual flood insurance is $12,000. Here is what you need to know.

What Flood Zones Exist in Redington Beach FL?

Zone VE: Coastal High Hazard Area (Gulf-Front)

Zone VE is FEMA's designation for areas subject to high-velocity wave action in addition to flooding. In Redington Beach, Zone VE encompasses the Gulf-front properties along the western shore of the island. Properties in Zone VE face the highest storm surge risk and the most significant wave action during hurricanes or major tropical storms.

Zone VE requirements for structures include: the lowest floor must be elevated above BFE plus any local freeboard, no enclosed space permitted below BFE (open pile or breakaway walls only), and elevation certificates are required. NFIP rates for Zone VE are higher than for Zone AE for equivalent coverage, and the NFIP $250,000 maximum often falls short of the replacement cost for high-value Gulf-front homes.

Zone AE: Base Flood Elevation Zone (Most of Redington Beach)

Zone AE covers properties at risk of flooding in a 100-year flood event (1% annual chance), with a defined Base Flood Elevation. Most of Redington Beach that is not Gulf-front falls into Zone AE, this includes canal-front properties on Boca Ciega Bay, properties near the Intracoastal Waterway, and most interior lots. Zone AE does not carry the wave action designation, but storm surge flooding is still a real risk on this barrier island.

Zone AE properties: lowest floor must be at or above BFE (Pinellas County may require 1-2 feet of freeboard above BFE for new construction), enclosed space below BFE is permitted but must have flood openings and does not count as living space, NFIP insurance is required for financed properties.

Zone X: Minimal Flood Hazard

Zone X (shaded and unshaded) designates areas outside the 100-year flood plain with minimal flood hazard. Very few properties in Redington Beach fall in Zone X. The barrier island's low elevation and exposure to Boca Ciega Bay and the Gulf mean that Zone X is rare here. If a listing claims Zone X status, verify it at msc.fema.gov before accepting that claim.

How to Look Up the Flood Zone for Any Redington Beach Property

Step 1: Go to msc.fema.gov (FEMA's Flood Map Service Center). Step 2: Enter the property address in the search bar. Step 3: The tool returns the relevant FIRM (Flood Insurance Rate Map) panel for that location. Step 4: Identify the flood zone designation and BFE for the specific parcel. Step 5: Note the effective date of the FIRM panel, older panels may not reflect recent remapping. Pinellas County community number for NFIP purposes is 125096.

For the most definitive determination, order a flood zone determination letter from a title company or flood determination service provider. These are standard in real estate transactions and typically cost $15-$30.

Private flood insurance has grown significantly in Florida since 2010, and many Redington Beach homeowners find that private carriers offer better pricing than NFIP, particularly for well-elevated Zone AE properties and for Zone VE homes needing coverage above the NFIP $250,000 cap. Always compare NFIP and private quotes with an elevation certificate in hand, the EC is what allows insurers to price accurately.

Hurricane Preparedness and Evacuation Zone A

Redington Beach is entirely within Pinellas County Evacuation Zone A. Zone A is the highest-priority evacuation zone, it is ordered to evacuate first when a major hurricane (Category 3+) threatens the coast. During a mandatory Zone A evacuation, Redington Beach residents must leave. This is not optional.

According to Pinellas County Emergency Management, Zone A covers areas at greatest risk from storm surge, which includes all barrier island communities including Redington Beach. Storm surge from a major hurricane can reach 10-15+ feet in Zone A areas on Pinellas barrier islands.

Hurricane preparedness for Redington Beach homeowners and tenants: Register for Pinellas Alert emergency notifications at pinellascounty.org/emergency. Know your evacuation route, Park Blvd east is the primary route; follow Pinellas County instructions as all causeways are used for contraflow during evacuations. Have 7 days of supplies, medications, and important documents ready. Plan for 2-3 nights minimum at a friend, family member, or hotel outside Zone A. Do not wait for a mandatory order to make your plan.

NFIP maximum building coverage is $250,000, high-value properties require supplemental private flood insurance.

Do I need an elevation certificate in Redington Beach?

An elevation certificate is not required to purchase a property, but it is extremely valuable. It tells you the exact elevation of the lowest floor relative to the Base Flood Elevation, which is the primary variable in calculating flood insurance premiums. For Zone VE Gulf-front properties, the relationship between floor elevation and BFE can mean a difference of thousands of dollars per year in flood insurance. Order one from a licensed surveyor ($400-$800) before making a final purchase decision.

What is the difference between Zone VE and Zone AE flood insurance?

Zone VE (coastal high hazard area) is subject to both flooding AND wave action. NFIP rates for Zone VE are generally higher than for Zone AE, and Zone VE construction requirements are stricter. Zone AE is subject to flooding without the additional wave velocity factor. Both zones require flood insurance for financed properties. NFIP policies have a $250,000 building coverage cap, Zone VE properties often need private supplemental coverage.

What evacuation zone is Redington Beach FL in?

Redington Beach is in Pinellas County Evacuation Zone A, the highest-priority evacuation zone, which is ordered to evacuate first when a major hurricane threatens. Zone A covers properties at the greatest storm surge risk, which includes all Gulf Coast barrier islands. When a mandatory Zone A evacuation is issued, Redington Beach residents are required to leave. Register for Pinellas County Emergency alerts at pinellascounty.org/emergency.

title: Moving to Redington Beach FL: What to Know
excerpt: Moving to Redington Beach FL: What to Know, Barrett Henry, REALTOR at REMAX Collective.
content:
Quick Answer

Redington Beach is a small barrier island community in Pinellas County with roughly 1,600 year-round residents, a quiet Gulf beach, and high insurance costs for waterfront properties. The closest grocery store is off the island. I'm Barrett Henry, Broker Associate at REMAX Collective. Call (813) 733-7907 to discuss buying in Redington Beach.

About Redington Beach

Redington Beach is an incorporated town on a barrier island in Pinellas County, Florida, between Madeira Beach to the south and Indian Shores to the north. The town sits in ZIP code 33708 and covers roughly one square mile of land area with about 1,600 permanent residents. The community is almost entirely built out, a mix of beachfront homes, canal-front single-family homes, and low-rise and mid-rise condominium buildings along the Gulf and the Intracoastal Waterway.

The Gulf of Mexico is the defining feature of daily life here. The beach is wide, public, and accessible. Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach is less than two miles south, offering restaurants, shops, dolphin tours, and a working commercial fishing fleet. The Intracoastal Waterway runs along the east side of the island, providing boating access north and south without crossing the Gulf.

What Redington Beach is not: it is not a walkable town for daily errands. There are no grocery stores on the island. Restaurants are limited. For most daily needs, residents drive to Madeira Beach, Treasure Island, or the US-19 corridor.

What Does It Cost to Move to Redington Beach FL?

Housing Costs by Property Type

Redington Beach covers a wide price range depending on location and property type. Non-waterfront condos in older buildings are the most affordable entry point. Gulf-front single-family homes represent the top of the market. The table below reflects general ranges based on recent sales activity in the area. Individual property values depend on floor height, building age, SB 4-D compliance status for condos, renovation level, and lot specifics.

Property Type Typical Price Range Notes
Non-waterfront condo$250,000 to $450,000Check SB 4-D reserve study and milestone report
Intracoastal/canal-view condo$350,000 to $700,000Floor height matters; higher units cost more
Gulf-front condo$500,000 to $1,200,000Building condition and HOA finances critical
Canal-front single-family home$700,000 to $1,400,000Dock, seawall condition, lot size affect value
Gulf-front single-family home$1,200,000 to $3,500,000+Zone VE; open pile foundation; highest insurance cost

Homeowners Insurance on a Barrier Island

Homeowners insurance in Redington Beach is significantly more expensive than inland Pinellas County. The wind and hurricane exposure on a Gulf-facing barrier island places properties in the highest risk category for most insurers. Many private insurers have reduced their Florida barrier island exposure, pushing buyers toward Citizens Property Insurance Corporation as the insurer of last resort.

For single-family homes, annual homeowners insurance premiums typically run $5,000 to $12,000 for non-waterfront properties and $10,000 to $25,000 or more for Gulf-front and canal-front homes. Wind mitigation inspections (around $150 to $250) can reduce premiums if the home has qualifying wind-resistant features such as hip roof, impact windows, or reinforced roof-to-wall connections. Always get insurance quotes before making an offer, not after, so you understand the full carrying cost.

Condo buyers pay into the building's master insurance policy through HOA fees. Verify that the building's master policy is current and covers adequate replacement cost. After several years of rate increases in Florida, some condo buildings have seen dramatic HOA fee increases driven by insurance cost alone.

Flood Insurance Costs in Redington Beach

Flood insurance is separate from homeowners insurance and is almost always required by lenders for properties in designated flood zones in Redington Beach. Most of the island is in Zone AE or Zone VE per FEMA flood maps. See the Redington Beach flood zones guide for full zone details and cost breakdowns by property location.

Flood Zone Typical NFIP Annual Cost Property Location
Zone VE$8,000 to $25,000+/yrGulf-front; open pile foundation required
Zone AE (canal-front)$2,500 to $8,000/yrIntracoastal and canal properties
Zone AE (interior)$1,500 to $4,000/yrNon-waterfront island properties

Under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 methodology, individual property elevation, construction type, and distance from water affect your premium more than the raw zone label. An elevation certificate ($400 to $800) helps insurers price your specific property accurately. Private flood insurance alternatives to NFIP are available and are worth quoting, particularly for higher-value properties where NFIP's $250,000 building coverage limit may be insufficient.

What Schools Serve Redington Beach FL?

Public School Assignments for ZIP 33708

Redington Beach falls within the Pinellas County Schools district. Children are assigned to schools based on their home address. Typical school assignments for the 33708 ZIP code are as follows, though assignments can change annually:

Level School Notes
ElementaryGulf Beaches Elementary Magnet120 121st Ave W, Treasure Island; magnet lottery required
MiddleBay Point K-8St. Petersburg; verify at pcsb.org
High SchoolBoca Ciega High School924 58th St S, Gulfport; (727) 893-2100

Gulf Beaches Elementary Magnet uses a lottery-based enrollment process for the magnet program. Applications open in late winter for the following school year. Families who do not win the lottery may be assigned to a different elementary school. See the Redington Beach schools guide for full details on the assignment process, private school options, and the PCSB school choice program.

Pinellas County School Choice Options

Pinellas County Schools operates an open enrollment program that allows families to apply to schools outside their attendance zone. Applications are accepted during the annual choice window (typically January through March). Acceptance depends on available seats at the requested school. Private school alternatives in the broader Pinellas County area include Shorecrest Preparatory School in St. Petersburg, Academy of the Holy Names, and Stetson University College of Law's campus in Gulfport for higher education.

What Are the Utilities Like in Redington Beach FL?

Electric, Water, and Internet Service

Duke Energy Florida provides electric service to Redington Beach. Average monthly electric bills run $130 to $220 in mild weather months and $280 to $420 in summer when air conditioning runs continuously. Single-family homes with older AC systems or poor insulation run toward the high end of those ranges. Contact Duke Energy at 1-800-700-8744 or duke-energy.com to establish service before closing.

Water and sewer service is provided by Pinellas County Utilities. Monthly water and sewer bills for a typical single-family home run $60 to $120 depending on usage. Contact Pinellas County Utilities at pcutilities.org to set up service. Natural gas is not widely available in Redington Beach; most cooking, heating, and water heating is electric or uses propane where installed.

Internet options include Spectrum cable internet (widely available throughout Pinellas County) and Frontier fiber internet in some areas. Spectrum's standard cable internet plans typically deliver 200 Mbps to 1 Gbps speeds. Remote workers should verify available speeds and providers at their specific address before committing to a property.

Setting Up Utilities When You Move In

Plan to set up utilities before your closing date so service is active on move-in day. Florida law requires new property owners to obtain a Florida driver's license within 30 days of establishing residence and register vehicles in Florida within 10 days. If you are making the home your primary residence, file for the homestead exemption by March 1 of the year following your purchase at the Pinellas County Property Appraiser's office. The deadline is strict; missing it means waiting another full year.

How Long Is the Commute from Redington Beach FL?

Commute Times to Major Employment Centers

Redington Beach access is via Park Boulevard (SR-694) going east over the causeway. This is the single connection to the mainland for the island communities between Treasure Island and Indian Shores. Peak-hour traffic on Park Boulevard and the approaches to US-19 can add 15 to 30 minutes to commute times. See the full Redington Beach commute guide for detailed route information.

Destination Off-Peak Peak Hour

Tampa CBD (I-275)45 to 60 min65 to 90 min
Tampa International Airport40 to 55 min60 to 80 min

St. Pete-Clearwater Airport (PIE)18 to 28 min25 to 40 min
Largo / Seminole12 to 22 min20 to 35 min

PSTA Transit Reality Check

Pinellas Suncoast Transit Authority (PSTA) operates bus service in the area, but service to and from the barrier island is limited and not practical for daily commuting to Tampa or downtown St. Pete. A car is essential for living in Redington Beach. Rideshare (Uber, Lyft) is available and reliable for occasional trips, but the daily commute to a Tampa-area employer requires a personal vehicle.

What Should I Know Before Buying in Redington Beach FL?

SB 4-D Condo Compliance for Buyers

Florida Senate Bill 4-D (2022) created new requirements for condominium buildings that are three stories or taller. Buildings must now complete milestone structural inspections and conduct reserve fund studies every 10 years starting at 30 years of age. Buildings must fully fund structural reserves (no more opting out of reserve funding as was common before 2022). These requirements have resulted in HOA fee increases and, in some cases, special assessments at older buildings throughout the Pinellas County barrier island communities.

Before buying a condo in Redington Beach, request and review: the most recent milestone inspection report, the structural integrity reserve study, the current reserve fund balance relative to the required amount, the most recent 12 months of HOA meeting minutes, and whether any special assessments have been voted on or are being discussed. I help buyers navigate this due diligence on every condo purchase I handle.

Elevation Certificate and Flood Zone Lookup

Every buyer of a single-family home in a flood zone should request the existing elevation certificate from the seller or have a new one prepared (a licensed surveyor prepares it for $400 to $800). The elevation certificate documents the lowest adjacent grade, the finished floor elevation, and any flood openings in enclosures below the base flood elevation. This information determines your flood insurance premium and whether the structure meets current FEMA standards. Look up the property's flood zone using the FEMA Flood Map Service Center at msc.fema.gov before making an offer.

Who Redington Beach Is Right For

Redington Beach is a good fit for buyers who want a low-key Gulf Coast beach community with a small year-round population, who can absorb higher insurance and carrying costs relative to inland Pinellas County, and who either work remotely or are retired. It is not well-suited for buyers who need a short commute to Tampa, who have school-age children and want walkable school access, or who want the amenities of a larger beach town within walking distance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Redington Beach FL like to live in?

Redington Beach is a small, quiet barrier island community on the Gulf Coast in Pinellas County with roughly 1,600 year-round residents. The lifestyle centers on the Gulf beach, the Intracoastal Waterway, and easy access to Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach. The trade-offs are real: no on-island grocery store, limited dining, high insurance costs on waterfront and Gulf-adjacent properties, and the need for a car for every errand. For buyers who want a low-key beach lifestyle without the crowds of Clearwater Beach or St. Pete Beach, it is a good fit.

What are property taxes like in Redington Beach FL?

Redington Beach is in Pinellas County and the Town of Redington Beach municipal taxing district. Total millage typically runs 16 to 21 mills depending on the property location and applicable special districts. A $500,000 home with the $50,000 Florida homestead exemption would generate an estimated property tax bill of roughly $7,500 to $10,000 per year. Look up actual millage rates and property history at the Pinellas County Property Appraiser site at pcpao.gov.

What flood insurance costs should I expect in Redington Beach FL?

Flood insurance costs vary significantly by flood zone and elevation. Gulf-front and Intracoastal properties in Zone VE typically cost $8,000 to $25,000 or more per year for NFIP coverage. Canal-front Zone AE properties run $2,500 to $8,000 per year. Interior Zone AE properties run $1,500 to $4,000 per year. Under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0, individual property characteristics drive pricing more than the raw zone designation alone. Get an elevation certificate and shop private flood insurers in addition to NFIP for an accurate cost picture.

What schools serve Redington Beach FL children?

Children living in Redington Beach are assigned to Pinellas County Schools. Typical assignments for the 33708 ZIP code include Gulf Beaches Elementary Magnet School at 120 121st Ave W in Treasure Island for elementary, Bay Point K-8 in St. Petersburg for middle school, and Boca Ciega High School at 924 58th Street South in Gulfport for high school. School assignments can change, and the Pinellas County school choice program allows families to apply to other schools in the district. Verify current assignments at pcsb.org using the school locator tool.

Is Redington Beach FL a good place to retire?

Redington Beach is a popular retirement destination for buyers seeking a Gulf Coast beach lifestyle with a small-town feel. The community is quiet, close to Pinellas County medical facilities including Northside Hospital and Palms of Pasadena Hospital, and offers easy access to St. Petersburg's arts and dining scene. The main challenges for retirees are the high cost of homeowners and flood insurance, the limited walkability for everyday errands, and the reality that some condo buildings are dealing with SB 4-D milestone inspection and reserve funding requirements that can mean special assessments.

title: Things to Do in Redington Beach FL
excerpt: Things to Do in Redington Beach FL, Barrett Henry, REALTOR at REMAX Collective.
content:
Quick Answer

The main draws in Redington Beach are the Gulf of Mexico beach, the Redington Beach Town Pier, and proximity to Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach (about 2 miles south). For restaurants and entertainment, most residents drive to neighboring communities. I'm Barrett Henry at REMAX Collective. Call (813) 733-7907 if you are considering buying here.

What Is the Beach Like at Redington Beach FL?

Gulf of Mexico Swimming and Sunbathing

The Gulf beach at Redington Beach is public, wide, and significantly less crowded than Clearwater Beach. The sand is white quartz and the Gulf water is calm and shallow for a long way out, making it a good swimming beach for families with young children. In summer, water temperatures reach 84 to 86 degrees F. In winter, temperatures drop to the high 60s to low 70s F, which limits swimming for most people but keeps the beach popular for walks and shell collecting.

Gulf Boulevard (SR-699) runs along the island with public beach access points at various cross streets. Street parking and small lots along Gulf Boulevard serve beach-goers. The town's small scale means beach access is never far from anywhere on the island. Dolphins are commonly spotted in the near-shore surf zone, particularly in the early morning and evening hours.

Redington Beach Town Pier

Redington Beach Town Pier at 17490 Gulf Boulevard is a landmark for the community. The pier extends over the Gulf and is a popular spot for fishing and watching the sunset. Species commonly caught from the pier and nearby surf include pompano, whiting, sheepshead, and seasonal Spanish mackerel. The pier area is also a reliable dolphin-watching spot. Confirm access rules and any applicable fees with the Town of Redington Beach, as they can be updated.

What Activities Are Near Redington Beach FL?

Johns Pass Village and Boardwalk (Madeira Beach)

Johns Pass Village is the most popular nearby attraction, located about 2 miles south of Redington Beach on Johns Pass between Madeira Beach and Treasure Island. The village has a working commercial fishing fleet, waterfront seafood restaurants, souvenir shops, outdoor bars, and a range of water-based tours. Dolphin watching cruises, sunset sailing trips, fishing charters, and jet ski rentals all operate out of Johns Pass. The Madeira Beach waterfront is accessible by boat or by car in 5 to 10 minutes from Redington Beach via Gulf Boulevard.

The pass itself (the inlet connecting the Gulf to the Intracoastal Waterway) is a notable landmark and a popular spot for watching boats navigate the channel. Fishing from the Johns Pass bridge is also popular, with snook, tarpon, and redfish among the species targeted by bridge anglers.

Indian Rocks Beach and the Pinellas Trail

Indian Rocks Beach is about 2 miles north of Redington Beach along Gulf Boulevard. The community is similar in character, with a quieter Gulf beach and a small selection of local restaurants along Gulf Boulevard. The Pinellas Trail runs along the mainland parallel to the Gulf islands and is accessible by crossing one of the causeways. The trail covers approximately 42 miles from St. Petersburg to Tarpon Springs and is used by cyclists, runners, and in-line skaters. Indian Shores and Indian Rocks Beach also have public beach access points that tend to be less crowded than Clearwater.

Kayaking and Paddleboarding on the Intracoastal

The Intracoastal Waterway on the east side of the island provides calmer water for kayaking and paddleboarding than the open Gulf. Mangrove-lined sections offer wildlife viewing opportunities for birds (including osprey, great blue herons, and roseate spoonbills during winter months) and manatees (particularly in cooler months when they seek warm water in power plant discharge areas). Kayak and paddleboard rentals are available from outfitters in the Johns Pass and Indian Rocks Beach area.

Where Do People Eat in Redington Beach FL?

On-Island Dining in Redington Beach

Redington Beach has limited on-island dining compared to larger beach communities. The commercial zoning along Gulf Boulevard and cross streets includes a small number of restaurants and casual dining options. The town's residential character means it has never developed a significant restaurant row. Residents typically drive to Johns Pass Village, Madeira Beach's 150th Street area, Indian Rocks Beach, or Treasure Island's Corey Avenue for more dining variety.

Dining in Neighboring Communities

The surrounding Gulf Beach communities offer a range of dining options accessible within 10 to 20 minutes of Redington Beach. Johns Pass Village has the most concentrated waterfront dining, with fresh seafood, casual bars, and family restaurants along the boardwalk. Treasure Island's Corey Avenue district has a mix of local restaurants and boutique shops in a walkable setting. For upscale dining, Gulfport and downtown St. Petersburg are 30 to 45 minutes south and offer a significantly wider selection.

What Are the Best Day Trips from Redington Beach FL?

Redington Beach's position on the Pinellas County barrier islands puts it within easy reach of a wide range of day-trip destinations. The table below shows estimated drive times from Redington Beach to popular destinations.

Destination Drive Time Highlights
St. Pete Beach / Pass-a-Grille15 to 25 minHistoric Pass-a-Grille neighborhood, Don CeSar hotel, Fort De Soto nearby
Fort De Soto County Park25 to 35 min1,136-acre park, top-ranked beach, camping, kayaking, Civil War fort ruins
Downtown St. Petersburg30 to 45 minThe Dali Museum, St. Pete Pier, Central Avenue dining, Mahaffey Theater
Clearwater Beach25 to 35 minPier 60, Sunsets at Pier 60 street festival, Sand Key Park
Caladesi Island State Park35 to 45 min (plus ferry)Undeveloped island accessible only by ferry from Honeymoon Island
Busch Gardens Tampa60 to 75 minTheme park with roller coasters and live animals
Gulfport Arts District30 to 40 minArt Walk (first Friday, third Saturday), Farmers Market, waterfront restaurants

Fort De Soto County Park

Fort De Soto County Park in Tierra Verde is one of the best outdoor destinations in the Tampa Bay area, consistently ranking among TripAdvisor's top beaches in the United States. The park covers approximately 1,136 acres across five interconnected keys, with a 7-mile multi-use trail, two beach areas, a fishing pier, canoe/kayak launch sites, campgrounds, and the historic Civil War-era Fort De Soto. The north beach is particularly well-regarded for calm, shallow water and soft sand. Day use access is free.

Downtown St. Petersburg

Downtown St. Petersburg, about 30 to 45 minutes from Redington Beach depending on route and traffic, offers a dense concentration of cultural and dining options. The Salvador Dali Museum at One Dali Boulevard holds the largest collection of Dali works outside of Spain. The Museum of Fine Arts at 255 Beach Drive NE covers European and American works. The St. Pete Pier is a public waterfront destination with restaurants, a museum of science, and programming. Central Avenue's restaurant and bar corridor runs for several miles through downtown and mid-town St. Pete.

What Seasonal Events Happen Near Redington Beach FL?

Annual Events Calendar

The Gulf Beaches area hosts a range of annual events within a short drive of Redington Beach. The Madeira Beach Wine Walk, Johns Pass Seafood Festival (held annually at Johns Pass Village and one of the largest outdoor seafood festivals in the Southeast), the Treasure Island Sanding Ovations sand sculpture competition, and the SHINE Mural Festival in St. Petersburg are among the most attended recurring events in the region. The Sunscreen Film Festival and the St. Pete Pride Parade (one of the largest Pride events in the South) take place in downtown St. Petersburg each spring. Gulfport's Art Walk runs on the first Friday and third Saturday of every month year-round.

For buyers interested in the lifestyle as much as the real estate, spending a weekend in Redington Beach and visiting Johns Pass, Treasure Island's Corey Avenue, and downtown St. Pete gives a much better feel for day-to-day living than any listing description can provide.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is there to do at Redington Beach FL?

The main draw at Redington Beach is the Gulf of Mexico beach, which is wide, clean, and less crowded than Clearwater Beach or St. Pete Beach. Redington Beach Fishing Pier offers free fishing access for town residents and paid admission for others. Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach is less than two miles south and offers restaurants, shops, dolphin tours, and a working marina. Water activities on the Intracoastal include kayaking and paddleboarding. The town itself has limited dining and no nightlife of its own; most entertainment comes from neighboring communities.

How far is Redington Beach from Johns Pass?

Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach is approximately 1.5 to 2 miles south of Redington Beach via Gulf Boulevard (SR-699). By car, the drive takes 5 to 10 minutes depending on traffic. Johns Pass is Madeira Beach's main commercial and entertainment district, with waterfront restaurants, souvenir shops, dolphin and sunset cruise boats, jet ski rentals, fishing charters, and a working commercial fishing dock.

Is there a pier at Redington Beach?

Yes. Redington Beach Town Pier is located at 17490 Gulf Boulevard. The pier extends over the Gulf of Mexico and is a local landmark for residents. Fishing from the pier is available, though access rules and fees may apply for non-residents. The pier area offers a good vantage point for watching sunsets and dolphin activity in the surf zone. Confirm current access rules and hours with the Town of Redington Beach, as policies can change.

What is the best time of year to visit Redington Beach FL?

March through May offers the most comfortable visiting conditions, with warm daytime temperatures, lower humidity, and calmer Gulf waters. The Gulf water temperature is warmest from July through October (80 to 86 degrees F), but summer months bring intense afternoon thunderstorms, higher humidity, and peak hurricane season (June through November). Winter months (December through February) are mild and sunny, with water temperatures in the high 60s to low 70s F, which some people find too cool for comfortable swimming.

Are there good restaurants near Redington Beach FL?

Redington Beach has limited on-island dining. The closest concentration of restaurants is at Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach, about 2 miles south, which includes waterfront seafood restaurants, casual dining, and bars. Indian Rocks Beach, about 2 miles north, also has a small collection of local restaurants. For a broader restaurant scene, St. Pete Beach's Corey Avenue and downtown St. Petersburg are 25 to 40 minutes south and offer significantly more dining variety.

Redington Beach (33708) is a small, fully built barrier island market. Non-waterfront condos start around $250,000. Gulf-front single-family homes reach $1.5M to $3.5M+. SB 4-D condo requirements are actively affecting buyer demand and pricing at older buildings. I'm Barrett Henry, Broker Associate at REMAX Collective. Call (813) 733-7907 for current market data.

What Is the Current State of the Redington Beach FL Housing Market?

Market Snapshot: Redington Beach FL (ZIP 33708)

Redington Beach is a small, fully built community with roughly 1,600 permanent residents and a limited annual transaction volume. With so few sales in any given period, individual transactions can move reported statistics significantly. For this reason, price-per-square-foot and comparable sales analysis by specific property type is more reliable than broad median price figures when valuing a specific home. The table below reflects general market characteristics based on activity in the area.

Property Type Price Range Typical Days on Market
Non-waterfront condo$250,000 to $450,00060 to 120 days
Intracoastal/waterfront condo$350,000 to $800,00045 to 90 days

Absorption Rate and Market Balance

With a small inventory of homes and a limited buyer pool relative to inland Pinellas County, the Redington Beach market can shift quickly between seller-favoring and buyer-favoring conditions depending on the number of active listings at any given time. At current insurance cost levels, buyers are taking longer to complete their due diligence, particularly for condo purchases requiring SB 4-D document review. Absorption rate for the single-family market is roughly 2 to 4 months' supply. The condo market absorption has been slower in buildings with open milestone inspection questions.

How Has SB 4-D Affected the Redington Beach Condo Market?

Milestone Inspections and Reserve Funding

Florida Senate Bill 4-D (2022), effective July 2022, created mandatory structural milestone inspections for condo buildings three stories or taller at the 30-year mark and every 10 years thereafter. Buildings also must conduct structural integrity reserve studies and fund reserves accordingly, with no more opting out of reserve contributions as was common before the law. These requirements were triggered in part by the 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse in Surfside, Florida.

Many Redington Beach condo buildings were constructed in the 1960s through 1990s, placing them in the age range where milestone inspections are required. Some buildings have completed their milestone phase 1 visual inspections with no significant findings. Others have undergone phase 2 engineering inspections that identified structural repairs, leading to special assessments. The range of outcomes is wide, building by building, and the only way to know a specific building's status is to review the documents.

What Buyers Should Ask for When Buying a Condo

Before making an offer on any Redington Beach condo, I recommend requesting and reviewing all of the following documents:

  • Most recent milestone structural inspection report (phase 1 and phase 2 if completed)
  • Structural integrity reserve study (SIRS) completed after July 2022
  • Current reserve fund balance relative to the fully funded amount in the SIRS
  • Most recent 12 months of HOA board meeting minutes
  • Current HOA budget and financial statements
  • Any pending or approved special assessments
  • Master insurance policy declarations page (coverage amount, deductibles)
  • Condo declaration and rules (to verify short-term rental policies, pet rules, rental restrictions)

A building that has completed its milestone inspection with clean results and maintains adequate reserves is in a fundamentally different position than one that is deferred on inspections or has a reserve fund deficit. That difference can mean the difference between a stable ownership experience and an unexpected special assessment of $10,000 to $50,000 or more per unit.

What Are the Seasonal Demand Patterns in Redington Beach?

Like most Pinellas County Gulf Coast communities, Redington Beach sees its most active buyer traffic from November through April, when northern buyers and second-home shoppers are most active. Listing inventory typically increases in the spring as seasonal residents who decide to sell put properties on the market. Summer listings often attract investors and buyers with more schedule flexibility, and motivated sellers sometimes offer better terms in the slower July through September period.

Hurricane season (June through November) adds another layer of caution for buyers who are unfamiliar with Florida's Gulf Coast. Properties under contract during active hurricane season may include inspection contingency language around storm damage. Buyers should build adequate insurance review time into their due diligence period regardless of when they buy.

Is Redington Beach FL a Good Market for Investors?

Long-Term Rental Yields

Long-term rental yields in Redington Beach are modest relative to purchase prices. A $500,000 non-waterfront condo generating $2,200 to $2,600 per month in rent produces a gross yield of about 5.3 to 6.2 percent annually before expenses. After accounting for property taxes (roughly $7,000 to $10,000/yr), insurance ($3,500 to $7,000/yr for a non-waterfront condo), HOA fees, management fees, and maintenance, net returns are often in the 2 to 3.5 percent range depending on leverage and specific property costs. Waterfront properties have higher purchase prices and higher insurance costs that compress net yields further.

Short-Term Rental Considerations

Short-term rentals in Redington Beach require a Florida DBPR vacation rental license, Pinellas County Tourist Development Tax (TDT) registration and 6% TDT collection, and compliance with local and HOA rules. A critical point: many condo buildings in Redington Beach prohibit short-term rentals in their governing documents. Buyers intending to use a condo for short-term rental must review the declaration of condominium and confirm no STR restrictions exist before purchasing. For single-family homes, the Town of Redington Beach may have its own STR ordinance; confirm with the town directly. If you are interested in rental income strategy, contact ViVi Property Management for guidance on the regulatory environment and property management options.

Browse homes for sale in Redington Beach. Check the live housing market for current listings and recent sales. See the Redington Beach investment property guide for cap rate estimates and rental strategy analysis.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current median home price in Redington Beach FL?

Redington Beach (ZIP 33708) is a small, fully built market where price ranges vary widely by property type and location. Non-waterfront condos trade in the $250,000 to $450,000 range. Canal-front single-family homes range from $700,000 to $1,400,000. Gulf-front homes can exceed $3,000,000 for the best lots. Median price figures for 33708 reflect a mix of property types and should be interpreted carefully when assessing value for a specific property type. For current comparable sales data, contact Barrett Henry at (813) 733-7907.

How long are homes sitting on the market in Redington Beach FL?

Days on market in Redington Beach typically run 45 to 90 days for single-family homes and 60 to 120 days for condos, with the condo market showing longer marketing times in part because of buyer caution around SB 4-D reserve and inspection requirements. Well-priced, turn-key properties in good condition sell faster. Properties in older condo buildings with unresolved milestone inspection issues or underfunded reserves tend to sit longer or require price reductions to attract buyers who are willing to take on that uncertainty.

How has SB 4-D affected the Redington Beach condo market?

Florida Senate Bill 4-D (2022) created mandatory milestone structural inspections and reserve fund requirements for three-story-plus condo buildings, and it has materially changed the Redington Beach condo market. Many older buildings on the island are in the 30-to-60-year age range where inspections are required. Some buildings completed inspections with clean results; others identified needed repairs and have levied special assessments to fund them. Buyers and lenders are scrutinizing condo financials more closely than before 2022. Buyers should request the full documentation package (milestone report, reserve study, HOA financial statements, meeting minutes) before making an offer.

Is Redington Beach FL a good place to invest in rental property?

Redington Beach allows short-term rentals in some zoning categories, subject to Pinellas County regulations, DBPR vacation rental licensing, and any applicable HOA or condo association restrictions. Many condo buildings in Redington Beach prohibit short-term rentals in their governing documents, so buyers intending to use the property as an Airbnb or VRBO must carefully verify the condo declaration before purchasing. Long-term rentals in the area generate modest yields given the high purchase prices and carrying costs. See the Redington Beach investment property guide for cap rate estimates by property type.

How does the Redington Beach market compare to Madeira Beach and Indian Shores?

Redington Beach tends to trade at slightly lower prices than Madeira Beach for comparable properties, in part because Madeira Beach has more commercial activity (Johns Pass Village), higher name recognition, and a more developed short-term rental market. Indian Shores, to the north, is a quieter community with slightly lower prices for non-waterfront properties and strong demand for its more residential character. All three communities share the same fundamental market drivers: Gulf access, barrier island lifestyle, flood zone exposure, and Pinellas County governance.

title: Tierra Verde Homes for Sale: Complete Buyer Guide
excerpt: Tierra Verde Homes for Sale: Complete Buyer Guide, Barrett Henry, REALTOR at REMAX Collective.
content:
Quick Answer

Tierra Verde FL homes for sale range from around $400,000 for non-waterfront properties to $2.5M+ for direct water-front homes with dock access. The island sits in Pinellas County near Fort De Soto County Park, with most properties in FEMA Zone AE requiring flood insurance. Call Barrett at (813) 733-7907 for current listings and local expertise.

What Is Tierra Verde FL?

Tierra Verde is a small, upscale island community at the southern end of Pinellas County, accessible via the Pinellas Bayway (State Road 679), a tolled causeway. The island sits between Tampa Bay and the Gulf of Mexico, directly north of Fort De Soto County Park and roughly 10 to 15 minutes from downtown St. Petersburg. The ZIP code is 33715.

The community is almost entirely residential, single-family homes, a small number of condos and townhomes, and a marina complex. There is no grocery store, no gas station, and minimal commercial development on the island itself. Residents drive across the Bayway for daily errands, typically to St. Pete Beach, South St. Pete, or Gulfport.

I have worked with buyers considering Tierra Verde over many years. The appeal is specific: island seclusion with real boating access, immediate proximity to one of Florida's top county parks, and a 10-minute drive to everything downtown St. Pete offers. The trade-offs are equally specific: flood insurance requirements, high homeowners insurance costs, limited walkability, and no on-island schools.

Tierra Verde FL Home Price Ranges

Tierra Verde FL Home Prices by Property Type

Property TypePrice RangeNotes
Non-waterfront SFR$400K-$700KInterior lots; no direct water access; lower flood risk on some parcels
Canal-front SFR$600K-$1.4MDock/lift access to Tampa Bay and Gulf; most common waterfront type

Gulf-front$2M-$5M+Very limited inventory; highest flood and insurance exposure

What Drives Price Differences in Tierra Verde

Water frontage is the primary price driver. Canal-front homes with a dock and direct boating access to Tampa Bay command a $200,000 to $500,000 premium over equivalent non-waterfront homes on the same island. The specific canal matters: wider canals with cleaner sight lines command more than narrow, winding canals. Properties with larger dock footprints and boatlifts for larger vessels sell at the top of the canal range.

Lot size is the second major factor. The island has a mix of modest lots from the 1960s and 1970s era builds and larger consolidated lots where owners combined adjacent parcels. Homes on larger lots with newer construction consistently outperform the older, smaller-lot inventory.

Why Buyers Choose Tierra Verde FL

The three reasons most buyers give me are: proximity to Fort De Soto County Park, direct boating access from their backyard, and the manageable drive to downtown St. Pete. The fourth reason, mentioned most often by relocating buyers, is that Tierra Verde feels like a private island community without being as remote or expensive as some barrier islands further south.

Tierra Verde vs. Nearby Waterfront Communities

Gulfport$300K-$900KLimited; bay access only some lots15-20 minPinellas CountyWalkable arts district; lower flood risk on many lots
South St. Pete$250K-$700KNo direct water access5-15 minPinellas CountyMost affordable; no island lifestyle

Fort De Soto County Park Access

Fort De Soto County Park is a 1,136-acre park encompassing five interconnected islands at the southern tip of Pinellas County, directly adjacent to Tierra Verde. According to Pinellas County Parks, Fort De Soto is consistently rated among the top county parks in the United States. The park contains two beaches (North Beach and Arroyo Beach), a 7-mile paved biking trail, two fishing piers, kayak and canoe rentals, a campground, and the historic Fort De Soto fortification dating to the Spanish-American War era.

For Tierra Verde residents, the park is accessible from Tierrra Verde Road with no Skyway toll. The combination of quiet residential streets, immediate park access, and boating from your backyard creates a lifestyle that is difficult to match in Pinellas County at any price point.

Flood Zone and Insurance Reality in Tierra Verde

Tierra Verde sits almost entirely in FEMA Flood Zone AE, which means flood insurance is mandatory for any property with a federally backed mortgage and strongly advisable for all buyers. Zone AE indicates a 1% annual chance of flooding (the 100-year floodplain), with base flood elevations established by FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Maps.

Flood insurance costs for Zone AE properties in Tierra Verde typically run $2,000 to $8,000 per year through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), depending on the property's elevation, whether it is pre-FIRM or post-FIRM construction, and the structure's first-floor elevation relative to the Base Flood Elevation (BFE). Private flood insurance alternatives are available and sometimes cheaper than NFIP for newer, elevated homes.

Combined homeowners insurance and flood insurance on a $700,000 Tierra Verde home can easily reach $12,000 to $20,000 per year. That adds $1,000 to $1,667 per month to the true cost of ownership above the mortgage payment. I always walk buyers through the true all-in monthly cost before we write an offer on any Tierra Verde property.

Buying Process for Tierra Verde FL

Step 1: Get Pre-Approved with Condo/Island Market Experience

Standard mortgage pre-approval is the starting point, but Tierra Verde buyers should confirm their lender has experience with island properties. Lenders need to evaluate flood zone designation, elevation certificates, and insurance cost estimates before pre-approving a realistic amount. The all-in monthly payment on many Tierra Verde properties looks very different from a standard inland pre-approval.

Step 2: Review Elevation Certificates

Every Tierra Verde property should have an elevation certificate on file or obtainable from the current owner. The elevation certificate documents the lowest floor elevation relative to the Base Flood Elevation. A home with first-floor elevation 2 feet above BFE pays dramatically less in flood insurance than one at or below BFE. Request the elevation certificate before making any offer and factor it into your insurance cost estimate.

Step 3: Inspect the Dock and Seawall

Canal-front properties have docks and seawalls that carry their own maintenance costs. A seawall replacement on a 50 to 75-foot canal-front lot can run $15,000 to $35,000 or more. A dock inspection by a certified marine surveyor is worth the $400 to $600 cost on any property with a dock and boatlift. Get the dock inspection before removing inspection contingencies.

Step 4: Verify HOA and CDD

Most of Tierra Verde is not covered by a comprehensive HOA. Some sections have deed restrictions or small voluntary associations. The community is not a master-planned development with CDD fees. However, waterfront section deed restrictions vary, so verify what restrictions apply to your specific parcel before closing.
