Park-and-Ride strategy: Some Redington Shores residents drive to a Park-and-Ride facility in Seminole or St. Pete and use PSTA or rideshare services for the final segment into downtown employment areas. This can reduce parking costs and driving stress for those with predictable work schedules. The Central Avenue corridor in St. Pete has multiple PSTA connections from Park-and-Ride facilities.

Is Redington Shores FL Good for Remote Workers?

Redington Shores is well-suited for remote workers, and the rise of remote and hybrid work has directly increased demand for barrier island properties in this area. The ability to live in a beach community without a daily commute is a major lifestyle upgrade for knowledge workers whose employers allow location flexibility.

Internet service: Spectrum (cable) and Frontier (fiber in select areas) provide reliable broadband to Redington Shores. Typical download speeds run 200-500 Mbps on cable and 500-1 Gbps on fiber where available. Internet reliability on the barrier island is generally good; the main risk is outages during and immediately after major storms.

Remote work lifestyle: During weekday work hours, Redington Shores is quiet. Beach traffic is minimal on weekday mornings. Local errands (grocery, coffee, pharmacy) require a causeway crossing to Seminole, but this is a 15-20 minute drive without rush-hour congestion. Many remote workers structure their day around morning beach walks, focused afternoon work, and evening local activities.

Coworking and coffee options: Redington Shores itself has limited dedicated coworking space. Seminole (10-15 minutes east via Park Blvd) and St. Petersburg (25-40 minutes) have multiple coworking spaces, libraries with workspace, and coffee shops suitable for occasional out-of-home work. For regular video calls, a reliable home internet setup is standard practice among remote workers in this area.

For buyers who are fully remote or hybrid (1-2 days in office), Redington Shores is a viable permanent residence. For buyers who need to commute to downtown Tampa 5 days a week, the 55-70 minute daily drive each way represents a meaningful lifestyle tradeoff to consider carefully.

Rideshare and Airport Transportation from Redington Shores FL

Rideshare (Uber, Lyft) is available in Redington Shores but wait times can be longer than in urban areas, particularly during late nights or early mornings. Surges during special events, beach season, and holiday weekends can make rideshare significantly more expensive from the barrier island.

For airport trips, many Redington Shores residents drive and park at TPA or PIE rather than rely on rideshare. Tampa International Airport (TPA) has multiple long-term parking options. St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport (PIE) is generally closer for Redington Shores and has lower parking costs. A car service booked in advance is another option many residents use for early morning or late night airport runs when rideshare availability is uncertain.

What Is Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores is an incorporated town in Pinellas County, Florida, located on a Gulf Coast barrier island between Indian Shores to the north and North Redington Beach to the south. The town occupies a narrow strip of land between the Gulf of Mexico to the west and the Intracoastal Waterway (Boca Ciega Bay) to the east, with Gulf Boulevard (CR 699) running the length of the island as the main road.

The town was incorporated in 1953 and has approximately 2,300 residents. It has the character of a quiet, established beach community, primarily owner-occupied single-family homes with a slower pace than the more commercial beachfront communities to the south (Madeira Beach, Treasure Island, St. Pete Beach). The lack of major commercial development in the immediate area contributes to Redington Shores' residential character.

Redington Shores is not a gated community and has no mandatory HOA for single-family homes. It is simply an incorporated municipality with its own small town government and services. There are no master-planned community amenities like clubhouses or community pools for single-family home residents.

What Types of Properties Are Available in Redington Shores FL?

The Redington Shores market breaks down into four main property categories, each with different price ranges, flood zones, and lifestyle characteristics:

Property TypeLocation on IslandTypical Price RangeFlood ZoneBoating Access
Gulf-front SFHWest side of Gulf Blvd; on the beach$1.2M to $3.5M+Zone VENo dock; beach and nearby marina

Single-family homes are the dominant property type. Condominiums exist in smaller multi-family buildings scattered along Gulf Blvd but do not dominate the market the way they do in nearby Treasure Island or St. Pete Beach. This skew toward single-family homes is one of the things that distinguishes Redington Shores from more condo-heavy barrier island markets.

What Drives Home Values in Redington Shores FL?

Understanding the value hierarchy in Redington Shores helps buyers prioritize properties and sellers understand pricing relative to the market.

Waterfront tier: Gulf-front is the highest value tier, commanding the largest premiums. Intracoastal-front is second, providing boating access and bay views without the Gulf-front flood insurance premium. Canal-front is third. Interior non-waterfront is the entry point to the market.

Lot size and water frontage: On Gulf-front properties, linear feet of beach frontage is the most valuable measurement. On Intracoastal-front properties, lot width (which determines how long a dock you can build and how large a vessel you can accommodate) is a primary driver. Larger lots command significant premiums in this fully built market.

Construction quality and age: Homes built after 2000 with current flood codes (elevated foundations, impact windows, coastal-grade materials) carry significant premiums over older 1960s-1970s construction. The Florida Building Code post-2004 (after Hurricane Charley) created a meaningful quality divide. Buyers should not assume that newer looking interior renovation negates the structural and insurance advantages of post-2000 new construction.

Flood zone and insurance cost: A Zone VE home with $20,000/year flood insurance carries a much higher effective ownership cost than a Zone AE home with $4,000/year insurance, even if the purchase price is similar. Smart buyers calculate total monthly carrying costs, mortgage + taxes + insurance, not just purchase price. Insurance cost is a legitimate differentiating factor between otherwise comparable properties.

Hurricane mitigation features: Impact windows and doors, hip roofs, and storm shutters reduce homeowners insurance premiums and qualify for wind mitigation credits. A home with a recent wind mitigation inspection and documented mitigation features typically pays $1,000-$3,000/year less in homeowners insurance than an otherwise identical home without them.

Redington Shores occupies the quieter end of the Pinellas barrier island spectrum. Buyers who want a true residential beach community with limited commercial development, predominantly single-family homes, and neighbors who actually live there year-round tend to find Redington Shores and neighboring North Redington Beach most appealing. Buyers who want more walkable dining and entertainment options within the community often prefer Madeira Beach, Treasure Island, or St. Pete Beach.

Buyer Due Diligence for Redington Shores FL

Buying in a barrier island market requires due diligence steps that buyers from inland markets often overlook. Here is what I walk every Redington Shores buyer through:

1. Flood zone verification: Look up the specific parcel at msc.fema.gov before making any offer. Know whether you are buying Zone VE or Zone AE and what that means for construction requirements and insurance costs.

2. Flood insurance quote: Get an actual flood insurance quote, not an estimate, before making a final offer. Flood insurance costs directly affect your monthly carrying cost and your financing options. Two or three quotes from agents who specialize in Pinellas coastal properties.

3. Elevation certificate: Request from the seller. If one does not exist or is outdated, order a new one from a licensed Florida surveyor ($400-$800). The elevation certificate is the key to understanding your true flood insurance cost.

4. Homeowners insurance quote: Standard insurers often do not write in coastal Pinellas. Get quotes from specialty coastal carriers and Citizens Property Insurance. This affects not just cost but also your loan approval, some lenders require proof of insurability before underwriting.

5. Seawall and dock inspection (waterfront only): Hire a qualified marine contractor to inspect any seawall and dock before closing. Seawall failure is expensive ($500-$900/linear foot to replace). Don't skip this inspection.

6. SB 4-D condo compliance (condos only): Florida SB 4-D (2022) requires condominiums 3+ stories to complete structural milestone inspections and fully fund reserves by specific deadlines. Request the building's milestone inspection report, reserve study, and current budget. Underfunded reserves can result in large special assessments.

7. Permit history: Pull permit history from Pinellas County to verify all work was properly permitted. Unpermitted additions or renovations can affect insurance coverage and create liability at resale.

What Does It Cost to Own a Home in Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores is a barrier island community in Pinellas County where property values and recurring ownership costs reflect both the desirable location and the real financial risks of coastal living. Understanding the full monthly cost before buying, not just the mortgage payment, is essential for making a sound financial decision.

The three major cost drivers that distinguish Redington Shores from inland Pinellas County markets are flood insurance, homeowners insurance, and property taxes. Together these three items can add $1,000-$4,000+/month to a mortgage payment that buyers initially calculate based only on principal and interest.

Property Taxes in Redington Shores FL

Redington Shores property taxes are calculated by Pinellas County Property Appraiser's office and include millage rates set by multiple taxing authorities. The total combined millage rate for an incorporated town like Redington Shores typically includes:

Taxing AuthorityApproximate Millage Range
Pinellas County (General)5.0 to 5.5 mills

On a $600,000 property with homestead exemption (typically reducing the taxable value by $50,000), the estimated annual tax bill would be approximately $8,800-$11,000. Without homestead (investment property or vacation home), the full assessed value is taxable, adding $800-$1,000/year on a $600K property.

Florida homestead exemption also activates Save Our Homes, which caps annual assessed value increases at 3% or the CPI, whichever is lower. This means long-term primary residents see their tax bills grow slowly even as market values rise. New buyers, however, are assessed at current market value, so the tax bill for a new purchase can be significantly higher than the prior owner paid.

Look up any specific property's current assessed value, millage, and tax history at pcpao.gov. Pay the current tax bill and review tax roll history before making an offer.

Flood and Homeowners Insurance Costs in Redington Shores FL

Insurance is the largest variable cost in Redington Shores ownership beyond the mortgage. The combination of flood insurance and homeowners insurance can add $800-$3,500+/month to carrying costs depending on property type and location.

Homeowners insurance (windstorm): Most standard homeowners insurers do not write policies in coastal Pinellas County. Coverage is typically obtained through specialty coastal carriers or Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, Florida's insurer of last resort. Expect $3,000-$12,000+/year for a single-family home in Redington Shores depending on age, construction type, hurricane mitigation features, and replacement cost value.

Flood insurance: See the flood zones post for full detail. Zone VE Gulf-front SFH: $8,000-$25,000+/year. Zone AE Intracoastal-front SFH: $2,500-$10,000+/year. Zone AE interior: $1,500-$4,000/year. How Are Property Taxes Calculated in Redington Shores FL?

Property taxes in Redington Shores are based on three components: (1) the assessed value set by the Pinellas County Property Appraiser, (2) applicable exemptions that reduce the taxable value, and (3) the combined millage rate set by all taxing authorities with jurisdiction over the property.

The formula is: (Assessed Value minus Exemptions) multiplied by (Total Millage Rate divided by 1,000). For a $600,000 property with $50,000 homestead exemption at 18 mills: ($600,000 minus $50,000) x (18/1,000) = $550,000 x 0.018 = $9,900/year.

Florida law requires the Property Appraiser to assess properties at 100% of market value as of January 1 each year, unless the property has an active homestead exemption that activates the Save Our Homes cap. New buyers should expect to be assessed at the full purchase price in the first full tax year after closing.

Actual tax bills depend on the Property Appraiser's assessed value, the specific millage rate for your tax year, and any additional exemptions or special assessments. Homestead Exemption and Save Our Homes in Redington Shores

Florida's homestead exemption is one of the most valuable tax benefits available to primary homeowners. For Redington Shores residents who make the property their primary residence:

Standard homestead exemption: Reduces the assessed value by $25,000 for all levies (county, school, municipal, etc.) for assessed values above $25,000. An additional $25,000 exemption (for assessed values between $50,000 and $75,000) applies to all levies except the school board. Combined, the standard homestead exemption reduces taxable value by up to $50,000 for most properties.

Additional exemptions: Florida offers additional homestead exemptions for senior citizens (age 65+, income-limited), surviving spouses of veterans or first responders, and veterans with service-connected disabilities. Contact the Pinellas County Property Appraiser to determine eligibility.

Save Our Homes cap: Once homestead is established, the annual increase in assessed value is capped at 3% or the Consumer Price Index (CPI), whichever is lower. In a market where home values rise 10-15% per year, a long-term Redington Shores homeowner with homestead can see their assessed value, and therefore their tax bill, grow very slowly. A new buyer purchasing the same property will see it reassessed at current market value, which can result in a dramatically higher first-year tax bill compared to what the seller paid.

I consistently tell buyers: do not use the current owner's tax bill to estimate your future property taxes. Instead, calculate taxes based on your purchase price using the current millage rate. The current owner may have owned for 10-20 years with Save Our Homes keeping their assessed value far below market.

Homestead Portability in Redington Shores FL

Florida homestead portability allows a homeowner who has accumulated a Save Our Homes benefit (the difference between market value and assessed value) to transfer up to $500,000 of that benefit to a new Florida homestead purchase within two years of selling the prior primary residence.

Example: A seller whose Redington Shores home had a market value of $1,000,000 but an assessed value of $400,000 has a $600,000 Save Our Homes benefit (capped at $500,000 portable). If they purchase a new Florida primary residence worth $900,000, they could apply the $500,000 portable benefit, resulting in a starting assessed value of approximately $400,000 on the new property instead of $900,000.

File for portability (Form DR-501T) when you file for homestead exemption at the Pinellas County Property Appraiser's office. The deadline is March 1 of the tax year for which you want the benefit to apply. Call the office at (727) 464-3207 with specific portability questions.

The difference between homestead and non-homestead taxes is modest in year one. But over 10 years in an appreciating market, a homesteaded owner's assessed value can fall far behind market, their annual tax bill can be $3,000-$8,000 lower than a non-homesteaded owner of an identical property. This is a meaningful financial advantage for those who use Redington Shores as a primary residence rather than a vacation home or rental.

Before making an offer: Pull both records for any Redington Shores property. Verify the market value the appraiser is likely to assign after your purchase, calculate taxes at that value using the current millage rate, and factor that into your monthly cost analysis. Never assume the seller's tax bill will be your tax bill.

Why There Is No New Construction in Redington Shores FL

Redington Shores is a barrier island community that was substantially developed between the 1950s and 1980s. By the time land values and building costs made development in other markets attractive, nearly every buildable lot in Redington Shores was already occupied. Today, the island is fully built, there are no vacant lots, no new master-planned communities, and no production homebuilders working in the area.

This is a characteristic shared by most of the Pinellas County barrier island communities: Redington Beach, North Redington Beach, Indian Shores, Madeira Beach, Treasure Island, St. Pete Beach. The supply constraint is one of the reasons these communities have seen strong long-term price appreciation. There is no way to add housing supply, so existing homes hold value relative to demand.

The only path to owning a brand-new home in Redington Shores is purchasing an older, typically smaller or less upgraded property and replacing it with new construction. This is called a teardown-rebuild, and it is the model that many buyers with custom home requirements pursue in this market.

The Teardown-Rebuild Process in Redington Shores FL

A teardown-rebuild project in Redington Shores has three phases: (1) lot acquisition, (2) demolition and permitting, and (3) new home construction. Each phase has significant cost and timeline variables specific to this market.

Phase 1: Finding and Acquiring a Teardown Lot

Finding the right teardown lot requires identifying properties where the land value significantly exceeds the value of the existing structure. In Redington Shores, these are typically 1950s-1970s era concrete block or wood frame homes on desirable lots, particularly Gulf-front, Intracoastal-front, or canal-front sites where the land value is $700,000-$1,500,000+ but the existing structure is worth $200,000-$400,000 in its current condition.

The negotiation for teardown lots is different from standard home purchases. Buyers are essentially buying land, so the condition of the house matters less than lot size, flood zone, setbacks, and FAR (floor-area ratio) limits that determine how large a new home can be built. I help buyers analyze lots for teardown potential including reviewing Pinellas County zoning for maximum building height, setbacks, impervious surface limits, and any deed restrictions.

Typical teardown lot prices in Redington Shores: non-waterfront interior lots $400,000-$700,000; canal-front lots $600,000-$1,200,000; Intracoastal-front lots $800,000-$1,800,000+; Gulf-front lots $900,000-$2,500,000+.

Phase 2: Demolition, Asbestos Abatement, and Permitting

Asbestos and lead paint abatement: Pre-1980s construction in Redington Shores almost universally contains asbestos (in floor tiles, drywall joint compound, pipe insulation, roofing) and lead paint. Florida law requires a licensed asbestos inspector to survey any structure before demolition, and licensed abatement contractors must remove hazardous materials before the structure is demolished. Abatement costs for a typical Redington Shores teardown structure run $5,000-$20,000 depending on the scope of contaminated materials found.

Demolition: Structural demolition of a typical 1,500-2,500 sq ft concrete block or wood frame home runs $15,000-$35,000 in Pinellas County, including hauling and disposal. Concrete block construction (common in this era) is more expensive to demo than wood frame. Budget $20,000-$40,000 total for abatement plus demolition on most Redington Shores teardowns.

Permitting requirements: New construction in Redington Shores requires Pinellas County building permits at minimum. Gulf-front properties within the Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL) setback require a Florida DEP CCCL permit, which is a separate state-level process typically taking 3-6 months. Zone VE construction must comply with FEMA Zone VE open-pile foundation requirements and cannot include enclosed habitable space below Base Flood Elevation. Zone AE properties must demonstrate compliance with Base Flood Elevation in the permit application.

Phase 3: New Home Construction

New construction costs in Redington Shores run $350-$550+/per square foot of living area, depending on quality of finishes, structural requirements, and whether the property is Zone VE or Zone AE. Zone VE Gulf-front construction is the most expensive because of elevated pile foundation requirements, impact-rated windows and doors throughout, and coastal-grade materials required for long-term durability in direct beach exposure.

Expect a Redington Shores teardown-rebuild to take 18-36+ months from lot purchase to move-in. Gulf-front projects with FDEP CCCL permit requirements typically land at the longer end of this range. Here is a realistic timeline:

Months 1-3: Property due diligence and closing; asbestos inspection; preliminary design and architect selection; begin permit applications.

Months 3-6: Abatement and demolition; Pinellas County permit processing (typically 3-6 months for new construction); FDEP CCCL permit processing (3-6 months, overlaps with county process).

Months 6-18: Foundation work and rough framing; MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in; inspections; enclosure (roofing, windows, doors).

Months 18-30: Interior finish work; final inspections; Certificate of Occupancy; landscaping and site work; move-in.

Pinellas County Tourist Development Tax (TDT): Pinellas County levies a 6% Tourist Development Tax on all short-term rental revenue from rentals of 6 months or less. STR operators must register with the Pinellas County Tax Collector and remit TDT monthly. Platforms like Airbnb and Vrbo typically collect and remit state sales tax but may not collect TDT, verify current platform remittance status.

SB 714 (2023): Florida SB 714 restricts local governments from enacting new short-term rental regulations stricter than those in place as of July 1, 2023. This generally protects STR operators from future local bans. However, HOA and condo declarations that prohibit STR are contractual restrictions, not local government regulations, and remain enforceable. Always read the full condo declaration and HOA rules before purchasing any condo for STR use.

What Types of Waterfront Homes Are Available in Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores sits on a narrow barrier island between the Gulf of Mexico to the west and the Intracoastal Waterway (Boca Ciega Bay) to the east. The island is roughly Gulf Boulevard running north to south, with properties flanking both sides. This geography creates three distinct waterfront property categories, each with different characteristics, price ranges, and practical considerations.

I have represented buyers and sellers across all three waterfront categories in Redington Shores and neighboring communities. Each type comes with its own set of advantages, costs, and due diligence requirements. Understanding the differences before you start shopping helps narrow your focus to properties that actually match your lifestyle and budget.

Gulf-Front Homes: Direct Beach Access

Gulf-front homes in Redington Shores sit directly on the Gulf of Mexico, typically with deeded beach access or a path to the sand. These are the most desirable and most expensive properties in town. They offer unobstructed Gulf views, the sound of waves, and walking access to the beach from your backyard or ground floor.

Gulf-front properties in Redington Shores are designated FEMA Zone VE, the highest-risk coastal flood zone. Zone VE construction requires open-pile or breakaway-wall foundations that allow wave energy to pass under the structure. Virtually all Gulf-front homes in Redington Shores that meet current standards sit elevated on pilings, with the living space well above ground level. Gulf-front insurance costs are the highest on the island: flood insurance $8,000-$25,000+/year, homeowners insurance $6,000-$15,000+/year.

Gulf-front properties do not have boat docks, the Gulf side is exposed to wave action and is not suitable for moored boats. Boaters who want Gulf-front living and boating access typically keep a vessel at a nearby marina (Madeira Beach and Treasure Island have multiple marina options) or access the water via kayak or paddleboard directly from the beach.

Typical Gulf-front price range in Redington Shores: $1,200,000-$3,500,000+ depending on lot size, linear Gulf frontage, home size, condition, and elevation. Larger lots with more beach frontage command significant premiums.

Intracoastal Waterway-Front Homes: Boating Access and Bay Views

Intracoastal Waterway-front homes sit on the east side of Gulf Boulevard, facing Boca Ciega Bay and the Intracoastal Waterway. These properties offer protected water access, dockable boats, and views across the bay to the mainland. They generally carry Zone AE flood designation, which is less restrictive than Zone VE and typically carries lower insurance premiums.

The practical advantage of Intracoastal-front living in Redington Shores is direct boat access from your dock. Boats can navigate north or south through the Intracoastal Waterway and reach open Gulf water via Johns Pass (approximately 2-4 miles south depending on your location) or the Blind Pass waterway. Travel time to open Gulf water by boat is approximately 20-45 minutes from most Redington Shores docks depending on vessel speed and route.

Intracoastal-front homes frequently have existing seawalls and docks. Dock size and boat capacity varies by lot width and water depth. Many lots accommodate vessels from 20-40+ feet with dock lifts. Some lots have floating docks that can accommodate larger vessels at high tide. Dock condition varies, older wood docks often need significant repairs or replacement.

Typical Intracoastal-front price range in Redington Shores: $700,000-$2,000,000+ depending on lot size, dock quality, home condition, and Intracoastal frontage.

Canal-Front Homes: Secondary Waterfront Access

A small number of Redington Shores properties sit on side canals that connect to the Intracoastal Waterway. Canal-front homes offer protected boating access at generally lower prices than Intracoastal-front properties, but canal width, depth, and distance to open water varies. Dock and Seawall Requirements for Redington Shores Waterfront Homes

Docks and seawalls are significant assets, and liabilities, for Intracoastal and canal-front waterfront properties in Redington Shores. Due diligence on dock and seawall condition is as important as the home inspection itself.

Seawall inspection: Hire a qualified marine contractor or structural engineer to inspect any seawall before closing. A visual seawall inspection typically costs $300-$600 and identifies cap damage, cracks, voids behind the wall, and signs of failure. Seawall replacement in Pinellas County costs approximately $500-$900 per linear foot installed. A 75-foot seawall replacement can run $37,500-$67,500 or more. Failing to identify a deteriorating seawall is one of the most expensive mistakes I see waterfront buyers make.

Dock inspection: Have a qualified marine contractor or inspector examine the dock structure, pilings, decking, electrical connections, and any installed boat lifts. Boat lift electrical systems in salt air environments deteriorate quickly and require regular maintenance. Unpermitted dock modifications are common, pull the permit history from Pinellas County to verify what was permitted and what was not.

Dock permitting: Any new dock construction or significant modification in Pinellas County requires permits from Pinellas County BOCC (Building + Permits), the Southwest Florida Water Management District (ERP permit), and in some cases the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Section 10/404 permit) and Florida DEP (environmental resource permit). The permitting process typically takes 3-9 months. Factor permitting lead time and cost into any plans for dock upgrades.

Flood Insurance for Waterfront Homes in Redington Shores FL

Flood insurance is mandatory for all financed waterfront properties in Redington Shores. The cost depends on flood zone, building elevation relative to Base Flood Elevation (BFE), foundation type, and coverage amount.

For Intracoastal-front and canal-front properties, an elevation certificate is the most important document to obtain before finalizing a purchase. The elevation certificate documents the lowest floor elevation versus BFE and is the primary input in determining flood insurance premiums. A building with a lowest floor 2 feet above BFE pays dramatically less than one at or below BFE. Order an elevation certificate from a licensed Florida surveyor ($400-$800) as part of your due diligence.

NFIP maximum building coverage is $250,000. Many Redington Shores waterfront homes are worth $700,000-$3,500,000+. Supplemental private excess flood insurance is needed to cover the difference between NFIP limits and actual replacement cost. Get quotes from both NFIP and private market carriers before closing. See the full Redington Shores flood zones guide for a complete insurance cost breakdown.

What to Inspect Before Buying a Waterfront Home in Redington Shores FL

Waterfront homes require more thorough due diligence than non-waterfront properties. Here is my checklist for any Intracoastal or Gulf-front purchase in Redington Shores:

1. Seawall inspection (marine contractor). Non-negotiable for any Intracoastal or canal-front property. Cost: $300-$600. Scope: structural integrity, voids, cap condition, tie-back assessment.

2. Dock inspection (marine contractor or inspector). Includes structure, electrical, boat lift (if any), permit compliance. Unpermitted work is common and can require restoration at buyer's expense.

3. Elevation certificate (licensed Florida surveyor). Determines flood insurance cost. Request from seller first, if existing cert is more than 5 years old or post-renovation, order a new one.

4. FEMA flood zone lookup at msc.fema.gov. Verify zone (VE vs. AE) and base flood elevation for the specific parcel.

5. Flood insurance quote (before making final offer). Get quotes from two to three agents. Compare NFIP vs. private market. Factor into your monthly cost analysis.

6. Home inspection (licensed Florida home inspector). Focus areas unique to barrier island homes: roof condition, window and door seals, HVAC (salt air accelerates corrosion; system may need replacement more frequently), plumbing, electrical panel for moisture and corrosion.

7. Permit history pull (Pinellas County). Search at epermits.pinellascounty.org for all permitted and recorded work. Unpermitted additions or modifications can create liability issues and affect insurance coverage.

8. Review of HOA/deed restrictions. Some waterfront properties are subject to deed restrictions or HOA rules governing dock modifications, boat size, rental, and landscaping.

What Flood Zones Exist in Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores is a barrier island community in Pinellas County, and virtually every property in town sits within a FEMA-designated flood zone. Understanding which zone a property is in before you make an offer is essential, because the zone determines flood insurance requirements, construction standards, and annual carrying costs.

According to FEMA flood insurance rate maps (FIRM), Redington Shores contains three flood zone designations. Gulf-front properties on the beach side carry the Zone VE designation, the most restrictive category. The vast majority of the town, including Intracoastal Waterway-adjacent properties and interior lots, falls in Zone AE. A small number of lots at higher elevations may fall in Zone X, which carries minimal flood hazard.

Zone VE: Coastal High Hazard Area (Gulf-Front)

Zone VE is FEMA's designation for coastal high hazard areas subject to both flooding AND wave velocity action during a 100-year storm. In Redington Shores, Zone VE covers the Gulf-front row of homes and any structures directly on the beach side of Gulf Boulevard.

Zone VE carries the strictest construction requirements: new and substantially improved structures must use open-pile or breakaway-wall foundations that allow wave energy to pass underneath the structure without transferring force to load-bearing walls. Enclosures below the base flood elevation in Zone VE are limited to parking, building access, and storage and cannot be converted to living space.

Flood insurance in Zone VE is the most expensive of any FEMA designation. A Gulf-front single-family home in Redington Shores typically pays $8,000-$25,000+/year in flood insurance premiums, depending on building elevation, foundation type, and coverage amount. Properties built prior to FEMA's original FIRM maps (pre-FIRM buildings) often face higher premiums because they may not comply with current elevation requirements.

Zone AE: Base Flood Elevation Zone (Most of Redington Shores)

Zone AE is the base flood elevation zone, covering properties subject to inundation during a 100-year flood event but without the additional wave velocity factor. The majority of Redington Shores properties, including homes on the Intracoastal Waterway side of Gulf Blvd and interior streets, fall in Zone AE.

Zone AE requires flood insurance for all properties with federally backed mortgages (conventional loans through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, USDA). The requirement cannot be waived. Annual premiums for Zone AE Intracoastal-front single-family homes typically run $2,500-$8,000+/year. Interior Zone AE properties often pay $1,500-$4,000/year, depending on building elevation relative to the Base Flood Elevation (BFE).

The relationship between the lowest floor elevation and the BFE is the key variable in Zone AE. A home with a first floor 2 feet above BFE pays significantly less than one at or below BFE. This is why an elevation certificate ($400-$800 from a licensed Florida surveyor) is one of the most valuable documents you can obtain before buying any Zone AE property in Redington Shores.

Zone X: Minimal Flood Hazard

Zone X (unshaded) designates areas outside the 500-year floodplain with minimal flood hazard. Very few properties in Redington Shores qualify as Zone X given the community's low-lying barrier island topography. Flood insurance is not required for Zone X properties with conventional mortgages, though many lenders and financial advisors recommend it. Private flood insurance for Zone X properties can be purchased for $300-$800/year in most cases.

How to Look Up the Flood Zone for Any Redington Shores Property

FEMA provides free public access to flood insurance rate maps through the Map Service Center at msc.fema.gov. Here is the three-step process for any specific property in Redington Shores:

Step 1: Address lookup. Go to msc.fema.gov and enter the full street address. The map will display the flood zone designation and the specific FIRM panel that covers the property.

Step 2: Request or obtain the elevation certificate. Ask the listing agent if an existing elevation certificate is on file. Many Redington Shores properties have had elevation certificates prepared for insurance purposes. If none exists, hire a licensed Florida land surveyor to prepare one. Cost is typically $400-$800. The certificate documents the lowest floor elevation, the base flood elevation, and other key factors that determine insurance cost.

Step 3: Get an actual flood insurance quote before closing. Contact two or three insurance agents who specialize in coastal Pinellas County properties. Request quotes under both the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and private market carriers. Compare annual premiums, deductibles, and coverage limits before finalizing your offer.

Pinellas County CRS Discount and Risk Rating 2.0

Pinellas County participates in FEMA's Community Rating System (CRS), which provides discounts on NFIP premiums for properties in participating communities. Depending on the CRS class rating for Redington Shores's specific NFIP Community ID, NFIP policyholders may receive a discount. Verify the current CRS class and applicable discount with your flood insurance agent, as CRS ratings change periodically.

FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 methodology, implemented in 2021, changed how NFIP premiums are calculated. Under the old system, premiums were based primarily on flood zone and elevation certificate data. Under Risk Rating 2.0, FEMA uses a broader set of variables including distance to water, flood frequency, property value, and multiple flood types (riverine, coastal, storm surge). For many Redington Shores properties, particularly Gulf-front and Intracoastal, Risk Rating 2.0 has resulted in significant premium increases over several years.

Existing NFIP policyholders are subject to annual premium increases capped by statute (typically 18-25% per year for existing policies), which means some policies are still transitioning to their full Risk Rating 2.0 rates. A policy with a $5,000 current premium may be moving toward a much higher rate over several renewal cycles. Ask the current owner or their insurer for the full-rates disclosure before assuming the in-force premium will remain stable.

Hurricane Preparedness and Evacuation Zone A in Redington Shores

Redington Shores is designated Pinellas County Evacuation Zone A, the highest-priority zone that is ordered to evacuate first when a major hurricane threatens the Tampa Bay area. Zone A covers all Gulf Coast barrier island properties, which face the greatest storm surge risk from a direct or nearby landfalling hurricane.

Storm surge, not wind, is the primary cause of hurricane fatalities and property damage on barrier islands like Redington Shores. During a Category 3 or stronger hurricane making landfall in the Tampa Bay area, storm surge of 10-20+ feet is modeled for barrier island communities. Many Redington Shores homes, particularly single-story structures, would be fully inundated in a major storm surge event.

When a mandatory Zone A evacuation is ordered, Redington Shores residents are legally required to leave. Remaining on the island during a mandatory evacuation puts both residents and first responders at risk. Pinellas County provides public shelter information and evacuation routes through its Emergency Management office. Register for Pinellas County Emergency Alerts at pinellascounty.org/emergency.

Practical preparation for Redington Shores homeowners includes: purchasing hurricane shutters or impact windows before hurricane season (June 1 through November 30), documenting personal property with photographs stored off-site or in cloud storage, maintaining flood and homeowners insurance current, and having a clear evacuation plan that does not rely on Gulf Blvd as it floods quickly in surge events.

Zone VE has both flooding and wave velocity action. Construction in Zone VE requires open-pile or breakaway foundations. Zone AE has flooding without the wave factor. Public beach access points along Gulf Blvd provide residents and visitors access to the Gulf.

I have worked with buyers relocating to Redington Shores from all over the country. The common thread is almost always the same: they want a genuine beach lifestyle, they are done with the inland sprawl they came from, and they are willing to accept the trade-offs (higher insurance costs, car dependence for errands, causeway crossings) in exchange for what they cannot get anywhere else: waking up 5 minutes from the Gulf of Mexico.

Who Is Redington Shores FL Right For?

Redington Shores is the right place to live if you want:

Beach walking, Gulf sunsets, and quiet residential surroundings as part of your daily life. The ability to kayak, paddleboard, or take a boat from your backyard (Intracoastal-front buyers). A primary or secondary home in a market with long-term supply constraint and consistent demand. Remote work or retirement flexibility that allows you to avoid or minimize daily commuting. A community that is primarily owner-occupied and relatively quiet compared to more tourist-heavy beach towns.

Redington Shores is not the right fit if you need:

Walkable access to grocery stores, restaurants, and entertainment without a car or causeway crossing. Short daily commutes by car to Tampa or even St. Petersburg (the drive is manageable but not short). Urban or suburban amenities and services at close range. Large-lot, new construction homes at lower price points (the island is fully built and prices reflect its location).

Setting Up Utilities in Redington Shores FL

Electric (Duke Energy Florida): Call (800) 700-8744 or visit duke-energy.com to establish or transfer electric service. Service typically starts within 1-2 business days. Have your property address, move-in date, and Social Security number ready. Monthly bills for a 1,500-2,500 sq ft home run $150-$400 depending on season and energy efficiency.

Water and Sewer (Pinellas County Utilities): Call (727) 464-4000 or visit pinellascounty.org to establish water and sewer service. Most Redington Shores addresses are served by Pinellas County Utilities. Service setup typically takes 1-3 business days and may require an in-person account establishment for new accounts.

Internet (Spectrum or Frontier): Spectrum (charter.com) serves most of Redington Shores with cable broadband. Frontier (frontier.com) offers fiber in select areas. Call ahead to confirm availability at your specific address. Monthly service runs $60-$100 for standard broadband packages. Self-install kits are available or schedule professional installation, which typically takes 3-7 days from order.

No natural gas: The Redington Shores barrier island has no natural gas infrastructure. All heating, cooking, and hot water systems are electric or propane. If your home uses a propane cooking range, contact a local propane delivery provider to set up a tank refill schedule.

Florida Driver's License and Vehicle Registration

Florida law requires new residents to obtain a Florida driver's license within 30 days of establishing Florida residency. You must surrender your out-of-state license to receive a Florida license. Visit a Pinellas County Tax Collector office with your current driver's license, Social Security card or number, and proof of Florida residency (lease, closing documents, utility bill).

Pinellas County Tax Collector locations include the Clearwater main office at 315 Court Street and branch offices in Largo, St. Petersburg, and other locations. For hours and services, visit taxcollect.com or call (727) 464-7777.

Vehicle registration must also be transferred to Florida within 30 days. You will need the Florida title (if your vehicle is owned outright) or title information from your lienholder, proof of Florida insurance, and payment of Florida registration fees. Florida's initial vehicle registration fees vary by vehicle type and weight. Florida does not require a vehicle inspection for registration transfer from another state.

Filing for Homestead Exemption in Redington Shores FL

If Redington Shores will be your primary residence, filing for Florida homestead exemption should be one of your first real estate priorities after closing. Homestead exemption reduces your taxable assessed value by up to $50,000 and activates the Save Our Homes 3% annual cap on future assessed value increases.

Filing deadline: March 1 of the tax year for which you want the exemption (e.g., file by March 1, 2025 for the 2025 tax year). If you miss the March 1 deadline, you will not receive the exemption until the following tax year.

How to file: Online at pcpao.gov, in person at 315 Court Street, Clearwater, FL 33756, or by mail. Required documents: Florida driver's license or Florida ID with your Redington Shores address, Social Security numbers for all owners listed on the deed, and the property's parcel ID number from your closing documents.

Portability: If you are selling a previous Florida homestead, file Form DR-501T (homestead portability) at the same time you file for exemption. Portability allows you to transfer up to $500,000 of accumulated Save Our Homes benefit to your new Redington Shores property. Call (727) 464-3207 with portability questions.

Insurance Setup When Moving to Redington Shores FL

Setting up the right insurance coverage is one of the most important logistics steps in a Redington Shores move. Coastal Pinellas properties require both homeowners insurance and flood insurance, and these are not commodities, the carrier, coverage terms, and deductibles vary widely.

Homeowners insurance: Most standard national carriers (State Farm, Allstate, etc.) have limited or no presence in coastal Pinellas. Your homeowners coverage will likely come from a specialty coastal carrier or Citizens Property Insurance Corporation. Secure homeowners insurance quotes before closing, lenders require proof of insurance commitment before funding. Annual premiums for a typical Redington Shores SFH: $3,000-$12,000+.

Flood insurance: Required for all financed properties in FEMA flood zones AE and VE. Obtain quotes from both NFIP and private market carriers. The flood insurance policy cannot be bound on a new closing until the 30-day NFIP waiting period has elapsed, this must be planned well in advance of your closing date. Annual premiums: $1,500-$25,000+ depending on property type and flood zone.

Moving the policies over: If you have existing homeowners policies from your prior state, those cannot transfer directly to Florida. You will need to apply for new coverage with carriers licensed in Florida. Start the insurance process at least 30-60 days before your anticipated closing date to allow time for multiple quotes and policy binding.

Healthcare Access from Redington Shores FL

The nearest major hospital to Redington Shores is Palms of Pasadena Hospital (1501 Pasadena Ave S, South Pasadena, FL 33707), approximately 15-20 minutes south via Gulf Blvd. Bayfront Health St. Petersburg (701 6th St S, St. Petersburg) is approximately 30-40 minutes southeast.

For major specialty care and trauma, Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital (501 6th Ave S, St. Petersburg) and Bayfront Health are the primary regional resources. Tampa General Hospital (TGH), the region's Level I Trauma Center, is approximately 55-70 minutes via I-275.

Primary care and specialist physicians are available throughout Pinellas County. St. Anthony's Hospital in St. Pete and Morton Plant Hospital in Clearwater are additional hospital options within 25-40 minutes. Healthcare access from Redington Shores is adequate though not immediately local, virtually all medical care requires a causeway crossing to the mainland.

Is Redington Shores FL a good place to live?

For beach lifestyle buyers, remote workers, retirees, and boating enthusiasts: yes. For daily long-distance commuters, urban walkability seekers, or budget-constrained buyers: the trade-offs are significant. The community is quiet, beautiful, and well-maintained but requires accepting car dependence and higher insurance costs.

Beach-centered and residential. The Gulf is the centerpiece of daily life, morning walks, sunset watching, paddleboarding, and boating from the Intracoastal side. The town is quiet on weekday mornings and more active on tourist-season weekends. No urban walkability; causeway crossings required for groceries, dining, and most services.

title: Things to Do in Redington Shores FL
excerpt: Things to Do in Redington Shores FL, Barrett Henry, REALTOR at REMAX Collective.
content:
Quick Answer

Redington Shores is a small Gulf-front barrier island in Pinellas County with direct Gulf beach access, the Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary two miles north, and Johns Pass Village five miles south for dining, fishing charters, and boat tours. Call Barrett at (813) 733-7907 for neighborhood guidance.

Activities and Attractions in Redington Shores FL: A Local Guide

Redington Shores is a quiet barrier island community of about 2,400 residents located between Indian Shores to the north and North Redington Beach to the south along Gulf Boulevard (SR-699) in Pinellas County, Florida. The town is intentionally low-key. There are no amusement parks, major hotels, or big-box commercial strips. What Redington Shores offers is Gulf of Mexico beach access, Intracoastal Waterway water sports, a handful of low-key local businesses, and quick access to the broader barrier island corridor.

I have worked with buyers and sellers on these barrier islands for over two decades. Most people who move to Redington Shores know exactly what they are getting: a small, residential beach town where the beach is the main attraction and neighbors still wave to each other. This guide covers what there is to do on the island and in the surrounding area.

What Does Redington Shores Actually Offer?

Gulf Beach Access

The Gulf of Mexico beach is the defining feature of Redington Shores. Public beach access points are located along Gulf Boulevard, and the beach itself is wide, clean, and significantly less crowded than Clearwater Beach or St. Pete Beach. According to Pinellas County Parks, the barrier island beaches have an average width of 100 to 150 feet, which gives swimmers and sunbathers room to spread out.

The Gulf water temperature runs approximately 60 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit from December through March, 72 to 80 degrees from April through June, 83 to 87 degrees from July through September, and 74 to 82 degrees from October through November. The calmer, shallower Gulf waters make this an easier beach for young children compared to Atlantic-facing beaches.

Intracoastal Waterway Water Sports

The Intracoastal Waterway separates the barrier islands from the mainland and runs the entire length of the island on the east side. This calm, protected waterway is ideal for kayaking, paddleboarding, and small boat cruising. Several rental operations along Gulf Boulevard and in neighboring communities offer kayak and paddleboard rentals. The Intracoastal is also good for dolphin spotting; bottlenose dolphins are common residents of the waterway year-round.

Fishing

Redington Shores itself does not have a public fishing pier. Intracoastal fishing is popular from kayaks and small boats, with snook, redfish, trout, tarpon, and sheepshead among the common catches. The nearest public fishing pier is the Indian Rocks Beach Fishing Pier approximately three miles north. For offshore Gulf fishing, charter boats operate from multiple marinas including those at Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach, about five miles south.

Buying or Selling in Redington Shores?

I specialize in Pinellas County barrier island properties. Call (813) 733-7907 for current listings and market guidance.

Contact Barrett

What Nearby Attractions Are Worth the Drive?

Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary (Indian Shores)

The Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary is located at 18328 Gulf Boulevard in Indian Shores, approximately two miles north of Redington Shores. According to the sanctuary's website, it is one of the largest wild bird hospitals in the United States and has treated more than 60,000 birds since its founding in 1971. The sanctuary maintains a permanent resident population of birds that cannot be safely returned to the wild, including pelicans, herons, egrets, osprey, roseate spoonbills, and owls. Admission is free, with donations accepted. This is a genuinely worthwhile stop and very popular with families who have young children.

Johns Pass Village (Madeira Beach)

Johns Pass Village is located in Madeira Beach approximately five miles south via Gulf Boulevard. The drive takes 10 to 15 minutes by car but can stretch to 20 to 30 minutes during peak season weekends. Johns Pass Village offers waterfront dining at multiple restaurants, souvenir and gift shops, dolphin watching and sunset cruise boats, deep-sea and inshore fishing charters, jet ski rentals, and a working commercial fishing dock. The Hubbard's Marina, John's Pass Seafood Company, and Bubba Gump Shrimp are anchor tenants. According to Visit St. Pete-Clearwater, Johns Pass Village is one of the most visited attractions in Pinellas County.

Fort De Soto Park

Fort De Soto County Park is located at 3500 Pinellas Bayway S in Tierra Verde, approximately 25 miles south of Redington Shores via Gulf Boulevard and I-275. The park covers 1,136 acres across five islands and includes a dog beach, two fishing piers, a kayak launch, bicycle trails, and the historic Fort De Soto fort dating to the Spanish-American War. According to Pinellas County Parks, Fort De Soto is one of the most visited county parks in Florida, drawing over 2.8 million visitors annually. The drive takes 30 to 45 minutes depending on traffic.

Sand Key Park (Clearwater)

Sand Key Park is a Pinellas County beach park located at 1060 Gulf Boulevard in Clearwater, approximately 12 miles north of Redington Shores. The park has a wide Gulf beach, restrooms, showers, parking, and a boat launch. It is less crowded than the main Clearwater Beach area because parking is limited to the park itself. The drive takes 20 to 30 minutes via Gulf Boulevard.

Caladesi Island State Park

Caladesi Island State Park is accessible only by ferry from Honeymoon Island State Park in Dunedin, approximately 20 miles north. The island has a pristine Gulf beach, hiking trails through mangrove forests, and kayak trails through the interior. According to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, Caladesi has been rated among the top beaches in the United States multiple times by Dr. Beach (Stephen Leatherman). The ferry ride takes about 20 minutes. This is an all-day outing rather than a quick side trip.

What Dining Options Are Available in and Near Redington Shores?

On-Island Dining

Redington Shores has very limited on-island restaurant options. The community is primarily residential and does not have a commercial dining district. Gulf Boulevard runs through the center of the island, and there are a small number of casual dining spots. Residents typically drive north to Indian Rocks Beach or south to Redington Beach and Madeira Beach for a broader restaurant selection.

Indian Rocks Beach (3 Miles North)

Indian Rocks Beach has a small but genuine local dining scene. Crabby Bill's Original (401 Gulf Blvd, Indian Rocks Beach) is one of the most recognized seafood restaurants on the central barrier islands and has been operating since 1978. Guppy's on the Beach (1701 Gulf Blvd, Indian Rocks Beach) is a local favorite for lunch and dinner with Gulf views. Sea-Guini (1500 Gulf Blvd, Indian Rocks Beach) combines Italian cuisine with seafood in a casual setting. The drive from Redington Shores takes 8 to 12 minutes.

Johns Pass Village (5 Miles South)

Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach has the largest concentration of dining and entertainment options near Redington Shores. Waterfront seafood restaurants, casual bars, and take-out stands line the boardwalk. For a more significant dining outing, downtown St. Petersburg is approximately 25 to 35 minutes south via Gulf Boulevard to I-275, offering a much wider range of chef-driven restaurants, craft cocktail bars, and entertainment.

What Is the Lifestyle Like for Redington Shores Residents?

Community Character

Redington Shores is a small town in the traditional sense. According to the U.S. Census, the town has approximately 2,400 residents on 0.9 square miles of land. There is no commercial center, no town square, and no major retail. The Town Hall is at 17425 Gulf Boulevard and handles local government functions. The community is predominantly owner-occupied single-family homes, though there are some condominiums in the southern portion near the boundary with North Redington Beach.

Who Lives Here

The resident population skews toward empty nesters and retirees who chose the island specifically for its quiet character. There is also a segment of vacation home and investment property owners who rent to seasonal visitors from late fall through early spring. Families with school-age children are less common given the limited on-island services, though Pinellas County schools are accessible via the Walsingham Road/Tom Stuart Causeway connection to the mainland. The community attracts buyers who want the beach without the noise and crowds of more commercial barrier island towns.

What You Give Up

Living on Redington Shores means accepting certain trade-offs. There is no on-island grocery store; the nearest full-service grocery options are on the mainland in the Seminole or Largo areas, accessible via the Tom Stuart Causeway. The closest major retail corridor is approximately 20 to 25 minutes east. Getting anywhere for daily errands requires a car. Evacuation Zone A designation means hurricane preparedness is not optional; residents need to understand their evacuation routes and be ready to leave ahead of major storms.

Day Trips and Excursions from Redington Shores

Downtown St. Petersburg (25-35 Minutes)

Downtown St. Petersburg offers museums (the Salvador Dali Museum at 1 Dali Blvd is internationally recognized), the St. Pete Pier, Tropicana Field (home of the Tampa Bay Rays), restaurants along Beach Drive and Central Avenue, and the Mahaffey Theater for performing arts. According to Visit St. Pete-Clearwater, downtown St. Pete has seen significant cultural investment over the past decade and is now one of the most vibrant small-city downtown districts in the Southeast.

Tarpon Springs (30-40 Minutes North)

Tarpon Springs is home to the largest Greek-American community in the United States and a functioning sponge-diving industry. The Sponge Docks on Dodecanese Boulevard offer sponge diving demonstrations, Greek restaurants, bakeries, and boutique shops. The Spongeorama Sponge Factory Museum is free. The drive from Redington Shores takes 30 to 45 minutes via Gulf Boulevard to Alt US-19.

Tampa (45-60 Minutes)

Tampa is accessible in 45 to 60 minutes via Walsingham Road to US-19 to I-275 N or via the Howard Frankland Bridge (I-275). Busch Gardens Tampa Bay, the Florida Aquarium, Amalie Arena (Tampa Bay Lightning), and Ybor City are major draws. Tampa International Airport (TPA) is one of the most convenient major airports in the state and adds to the practical appeal of the barrier island location.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is there to do in Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores is a small Gulf-front barrier island community with about 2,400 residents. The primary draw is the Gulf of Mexico beach, with public beach access along Gulf Boulevard. The Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary in neighboring Indian Shores is two miles north and is one of the largest wild bird hospitals in the United States. For dining, shopping, dolphin tours, and fishing charters, Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach is approximately five miles south via Gulf Boulevard and takes 10 to 15 minutes by car. The Intracoastal Waterway on the east side of the island is popular for kayaking and paddleboarding.

Q: Is there a fishing pier in Redington Shores?

Redington Shores does not have its own fishing pier. The nearest public fishing piers are the Indian Rocks Beach Fishing Pier in Indian Rocks Beach (approximately three miles north) and piers at Fort De Soto Park (about 25 miles south via I-275). Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach, five miles south, has fishing charter boats and party boat fishing available through multiple operators. Intracoastal fishing from kayaks or small boats is also popular along the west side of the waterway.

Q: How far is Redington Shores from Johns Pass Village?

Johns Pass Village in Madeira Beach is approximately five to six miles south of Redington Shores via Gulf Boulevard (SR-699). The drive typically takes 10 to 15 minutes depending on traffic, which can be heavy on weekends during season (November through April). Johns Pass Village offers waterfront dining, souvenir shops, dolphin and sunset cruise boats, jet ski rentals, fishing charters, and a working commercial fishing dock. It is the largest commercial and entertainment node on the central Pinellas barrier islands.

Q: What beaches are near Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores has direct Gulf of Mexico beach access with public access points along Gulf Boulevard. Indian Shores beach is immediately to the north. Redington Beach and North Redington Beach are just to the south, accessible within a five-minute drive via Gulf Boulevard. Sand Key Park in Clearwater is approximately 12 miles north and is a popular county beach park with restrooms and parking. Clearwater Beach, rated consistently among the top beaches in the United States, is about 15 miles north and takes 25 to 35 minutes to reach.

Q: What is the Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary near Redington Shores?

The Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary is located at 18328 Gulf Boulevard in Indian Shores, approximately two miles north of Redington Shores. It is one of the largest wild bird hospitals in the United States and operates as a nonprofit organization. The sanctuary treats injured wild birds including pelicans, herons, egrets, osprey, and owls, and maintains a permanent resident population of birds that cannot be released into the wild. Admission is free, though donations are welcomed. It is a genuine local attraction that is very different from typical tourist sites.

title: Redington Shores FL Housing Market Overview
excerpt: Redington Shores FL Housing Market Overview, Barrett Henry, REALTOR at REMAX Collective.
content:
Quick Answer

Redington Shores is a supply-constrained barrier island market with about 900 to 1,000 homes. No new construction land exists, which supports long-term values. Interior SFH prices range from $450K to $800K; Intracoastal canal-front runs $700K to $1.5M; Gulf-front commands $1.5M to $5M+. Call Barrett at (813) 733-7907 for current market guidance.

Redington Shores FL Housing Market: Price Tiers, Inventory, and What Buyers Need to Know

Redington Shores is one of the smallest incorporated towns on Florida's Gulf Coast. The town covers 0.9 square miles on a barrier island in Pinellas County, bounded by the Gulf of Mexico to the west and the Intracoastal Waterway to the east. With roughly 900 to 1,000 residential units and no developable vacant land, this is a closed-inventory market. When you are evaluating a purchase here, you are not comparing against a sprawling suburban market where new subdivisions periodically reset price expectations. You are buying into a fixed stock of homes that has not grown in decades.

I have sold properties on these barrier islands for over 20 years. The fundamental characteristic of Redington Shores, and barrier island markets in general, is supply scarcity combined with premium demand. That combination creates different market dynamics than you see in inland suburban markets. This guide breaks down the current market structure, price tiers, seasonal patterns, and what buyers need to understand before making an offer.

What Are the Key Supply Constraints in Redington Shores?

No Vacant Land for New Construction

Redington Shores is fully built out. According to Pinellas County Property Appraiser records, there are no vacant platted residential lots available in Redington Shores for conventional new construction. The only path to a "new" home on the island is a teardown-rebuild: buying an existing structure, demolishing it, and building new in its place. This process involves FDEP (Florida Department of Environmental Protection) Coastal Construction Control Line (CCCL) permits for any Gulf-adjacent lot, Army Corps of Engineers wetlands review for waterfront properties, and standard Pinellas County building permits. The all-in cost of a teardown-rebuild in Redington Shores typically runs $1.5 million to $3.5 million or more depending on lot type and finished home specifications. See the new construction guide for a full teardown-rebuild cost breakdown.

Small Total Inventory

With approximately 900 to 1,000 total residential units and a typical annual sales volume of 40 to 70 transactions, the absorption rate in Redington Shores is low relative to larger markets. This means that when a well-priced property comes to market, the buyer pool is comparatively deep against the supply. It also means that poorly priced or condition-challenged properties can sit for months because buyers have limited urgency when the total available inventory is thin.

Insurance and Financing Headwinds

The most significant market headwind in Redington Shores is not a lack of buyer demand; it is the cost and availability of property insurance. Since 2022, multiple private carriers have reduced their presence in the Florida coastal insurance market. According to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, several major carriers have non-renewed or not renewed coastal property policies across Pinellas County. This forces many buyers into Citizens Property Insurance Corporation (the state-backed insurer of last resort) or specialty carriers at significantly higher premiums. A full insurance cost analysis, including homeowners, flood (separate policy), and wind (which may be separate from HO depending on carrier), is an essential step in evaluating any Redington Shores purchase.

Market Questions? I Can Help.

23+ years of barrier island real estate experience. Call (813) 733-7907 for a current market briefing.

Contact Barrett

What Do Homes Cost in Redington Shores?

Price Tier Breakdown

Redington Shores prices are driven by three factors: waterfront access (Gulf-front commands the highest premium, canal/Intracoastal second), condition and renovation level, and flood zone designation. The price tiers below are general ranges based on market observations; individual properties vary based on lot size, elevation, views, and condition.

What Drives the Price Premium Over Mainland Markets?

An interior Redington Shores home at $500,000 to $700,000 is approximately 50% to 100% more expensive than a comparable mainland Pinellas home at similar finishes. The premium reflects three components: location (Gulf-front barrier island within Pinellas County, close to everything Tampa Bay offers), scarcity (no new supply can enter), and lifestyle (walking distance to the Gulf). Buyers should verify that the specific property they are considering actually delivers on the scarcity premium. An interior home four blocks from the nearest beach access point is not the same as a Gulf-front home, even though both carry a barrier island address.

What Are the Seasonal Market Patterns?

Peak Season: January Through April

The strongest buyer activity on the Pinellas barrier islands occurs from January through April. This is when seasonal residents from the Northeast and Midwest are in the area, and when the combination of mild weather and high visibility in the market brings out the most motivated buyers. Well-priced properties listed in January or February often receive multiple showing requests within the first two weeks. Sellers who want top dollar should target this window for listing.

Summer Slowdown: May Through September

Summer brings high heat, humidity, daily thunderstorms, and hurricane season (June through November). Buyer traffic drops noticeably from May through September, and properties that did not sell during the spring peak may require price adjustments to attract off-season buyers. This is not a distressed market dynamic; it is a seasonal reality of coastal Florida that experienced buyers understand. For buyers who have the flexibility to purchase off-season, competition is lower and negotiating leverage is somewhat better.

Fall Second Wave: October Through December

October through December represents a second wave of buyer activity as snowbirds arrive and northern buyers make pre-season purchases before the January rush. Properties that have been sitting since the spring peak sometimes attract re-energized interest in this window if sellers adjust pricing to reflect the market reality from the slower summer months.

Madeira Beach and Clearwater Beach are more commercial and attract more tourist traffic, which translates to stronger STR performance but a different day-to-day living experience for full-time residents.

What Should Buyers Know Before Making an Offer?

Elevation Certificate Is Essential

Before making an offer on any Redington Shores property, request the existing elevation certificate if one is on file, or budget for a new one ($450 to $750 from a licensed surveyor). The elevation certificate determines flood insurance cost under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 pricing system and is one of the most important documents in a coastal property transaction. A home that appears attractively priced may be unattractive once the annual flood insurance premium is factored into the total cost of ownership.

Insurance Cost Analysis Before Under Contract

Do not wait until you are under contract to get insurance quotes. The current Florida insurance market requires buyers to engage an independent insurance agent early in the search process. Get a homeowners insurance quote, a separate flood insurance quote (NFIP or private), and a wind mitigation inspection for any property built before 2001. For properties in Zone VE, budget $12,000 to $30,000 per year or more for the combined insurance cost depending on coverage levels and property value. This is a carrying cost that affects investment returns and affordability calculations.

Condo Due Diligence Under SB 4-D

Florida Senate Bill 4-D, signed into law in 2022 and with mandatory compliance deadlines in 2025, requires condominium associations to maintain fully funded structural reserves and complete milestone inspections for buildings three stories or more that are 25 years old or older. For Redington Shores condominiums, buyers must request the most recent milestone inspection report, the structural integrity reserve study, current reserve funding levels, and the last three years of HOA financial statements and meeting minutes. Special assessments and HOA fee increases to fund required reserves have been significant in some complexes. See the investment property guide for detailed SB 4-D buyer checklist.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the housing market like in Redington Shores FL?

Redington Shores is a supply-constrained barrier island market with approximately 900 to 1,000 homes on 0.9 square miles. There is no undeveloped land for new construction; growth can only come from teardown-rebuild or renovation. This structural scarcity supports long-term values. Homes range from interior single-family residences priced around $450,000 to $800,000 to Intracoastal canal-front properties at $700,000 to $1.5 million and Gulf-front homes at $1.5 million to over $5 million. Insurance costs have increased significantly since 2022, which has affected affordability and buyer qualification thresholds.

Q: Are home prices going up or down in Redington Shores?

Barrier island markets like Redington Shores tend to experience less volatility than mainland suburban markets because the supply of homes is physically fixed. When buyer demand increases, prices rise more sharply than on the mainland because no new supply can enter the market. When demand softens, prices compress rather than collapse because there are no distressed subdivisions dumping inventory. The primary risk factors for Redington Shores values are hurricane damage events, insurance availability and cost, and changes to federal flood insurance program structures. Buyers should evaluate each property's specific flood zone, elevation, and insurance cost history before making decisions based on price comparisons alone.

Q: How long do homes stay on the market in Redington Shores?

Days on market in Redington Shores varies significantly by price tier and property type. Well-priced interior single-family homes at $450,000 to $750,000 in good condition can go under contract within 30 to 60 days when listed during the January through April buying season. Waterfront properties, particularly Gulf-front homes above $1.5 million, can take 60 to 180 days or longer because the buyer pool at those price points is smaller and more deliberate. Properties with deferred maintenance, outdated systems, or in higher flood-risk zones (Zone VE) tend to sit longer as buyers factor in the cost to address those issues.

Q: Is Redington Shores a good investment for rental property?

Redington Shores is a viable short-term rental (STR) market given its Gulf-front location. Pinellas County requires an STR registration and the Florida DBPR vacation rental license (Form DBPR HR-7001). Pinellas County also collects a 6% Tourist Development Tax (TDT) in addition to Florida sales tax. Gulf-adjacent homes with beach access command higher nightly rates and occupancy. The realistic gross annual STR revenue for a well-situated 3-bedroom home ranges from $60,000 to $120,000 depending on proximity to the beach, condition, and amenities. Net returns after insurance, mortgage, taxes, management fees, and maintenance are typically lower than gross numbers suggest. Consult ViVi Property Management at nowtb.com/property-management/ for current Pinellas County STR management rates and performance data.

Q: What should buyers know about flood insurance in Redington Shores?

Most properties in Redington Shores fall within FEMA Flood Zone AE or VE on Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs). Zone VE is the highest-risk designation applied to Gulf-front properties and requires elevation above base flood elevation plus freeboard, and NFIP or private flood insurance. Annual NFIP flood premiums for Zone VE properties can run $8,000 to $25,000 or more depending on elevation, coverage amount, and property characteristics under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 pricing system (implemented October 2021). Zone AE canal-front and interior properties typically have lower premiums in the $2,000 to $8,000 range for the structure, though private flood insurance can sometimes be more competitive. An elevation certificate, ordered from a licensed surveyor for $450 to $750, is essential for any Redington Shores purchase to understand the true insurance cost.
